leads.title: Abraham smashes the idols
leads.summary: In Genesis Rabbah, Abraham smashes the idols in his father's shop, blames the largest one, and is thrown into a furnace by Nimrod. In the Quran, Abraham breaks the idols except the biggest, tells the people to ask them, and is thrown into a fire made cool.

leads.title: The Buddha becomes a Christian saint
leads.summary: The life of the Buddha passed through Manichaean and Arabic versions (Bilawhar wa-Būdhāsf) into the Georgian Balavariani and the Greek Barlaam and Ioasaph. Josaphat became a saint in the Christian calendar.

evidence.text: The name chain bodhisattva → Būdhāsaf → Yūdāsaf → Iōasaph is the lexical spine of the lead.

leads.title: The raven that teaches burial
leads.summary: In the Quran a raven shows Cain how to bury Abel. In Pirqei de-Rabbi Eliezer a raven shows Adam and Eve.

passages.text: فَبَعَثَ ٱللَّهُ غُرَابًا يَبْحَثُ فِى ٱلْأَرْضِ لِيُرِيَهُۥ كَيْفَ يُوَٰرِى سَوْءَةَ أَخِيهِ قَالَ يَٰوَيْلَتَىٰٓ أَعَجَزْتُ أَنْ أَكُونَ مِثْلَ هَٰذَا ٱلْغُرَابِ فَأُوَٰرِىَ سَوْءَةَ أَخِى فَأَصْبَحَ مِنَ ٱلنَّٰدِمِينَ

leads.title: Jesus brings clay birds to life
leads.summary: In the Infancy Gospel of Thomas the child Jesus shapes sparrows from clay and makes them fly. The Quran has Jesus fashion birds from clay that become birds by God's permission.

passages.text: (3:49) وَرَسُولًا إِلَىٰ بَنِىٓ إِسْرَٰٓءِيلَ أَنِّى قَدْ جِئْتُكُم بِـَٔايَةٍ مِّن رَّبِّكُمْ أَنِّىٓ أَخْلُقُ لَكُم مِّنَ ٱلطِّينِ كَهَيْـَٔةِ ٱلطَّيْرِ فَأَنفُخُ فِيهِ فَيَكُونُ طَيْرًۢا بِإِذْنِ ٱللَّهِ وَأُبْرِئُ ٱلْأَكْمَهَ وَٱلْأَبْرَصَ وَأُحْىِ ٱلْمَوْتَىٰ بِإِذْنِ ٱللَّهِ وَأُنَبِّئُكُم بِمَا تَأْكُلُونَ وَمَا تَدَّخِرُونَ فِى بُيُوتِكُمْ إِنَّ فِى ذَٰلِكَ لَءَايَةً لَّكُمْ إِن كُنتُم مُّؤْمِنِينَ (5:110) إِذْ قَالَ ٱللَّهُ يَٰعِيسَى ٱبْنَ مَرْيَمَ ٱذْكُرْ نِعْمَتِى عَلَيْكَ وَعَلَىٰ وَٰلِدَتِكَ إِذْ أَيَّدتُّكَ بِرُوحِ ٱلْقُدُسِ تُكَلِّمُ ٱلنَّاسَ فِى ٱلْمَهْدِ وَكَهْلًا وَإِذْ عَلَّمْتُكَ ٱلْكِتَٰبَ وَٱلْحِكْمَةَ وَٱلتَّوْرَىٰةَ وَٱلْإِنجِيلَ وَإِذْ تَخْلُقُ مِنَ ٱلطِّينِ كَهَيْـَٔةِ ٱلطَّيْرِ بِإِذْنِى فَتَنفُخُ فِيهَا فَتَكُونُ طَيْرًۢا بِإِذْنِى وَتُبْرِئُ ٱلْأَكْمَهَ وَٱلْأَبْرَصَ بِإِذْنِى وَإِذْ تُخْرِجُ ٱلْمَوْتَىٰ بِإِذْنِى وَإِذْ كَفَفْتُ بَنِىٓ إِسْرَٰٓءِيلَ عَنكَ إِذْ جِئْتَهُم بِٱلْبَيِّنَٰتِ فَقَالَ ٱلَّذِينَ كَفَرُوا۟ مِنْهُمْ إِنْ هَٰذَآ إِلَّا سِحْرٌ مُّبِينٌ

leads.title: Dhul-Qarnayn and the Alexander legends
leads.summary: The Quran's Dhul-Qarnayn travels to where the sun sets and rises and builds a barrier against Gog and Magog. The Syriac Alexander Legend and the Alexander Romance have close parallels.

passages.text_omitted: longer than 12 verses; read it in the source

evidence.text: The Syriac Legend is often dated around 630 (Reinink), close to the Quran. The direction and the dating are both debated.

leads.title: Flood narratives across traditions
leads.summary: A divinely sent flood with a chosen survivor appears in Sumerian, Akkadian, Hebrew, Quranic, Vedic, Greek, and Chinese sources. The Near Eastern versions are historically linked; the others are candidate convergences.

passages.text_omitted: longer than 12 verses; read it in the source

passages.ref: Shujing; Mencius (Gun and Yu tame the flood)

evidence.text: Specificity test: the bird-release sequence (Gilgamesh XI; Genesis 8) is a rare motif combination that marks the Mesopotamian–Hebrew link. The Quran has no bird release.
Noah's drowned son (Quran 11:42–43) has no Genesis counterpart and is a sub-lead.
The Chinese story is about controlling the flood, not surviving it, so it is a weak match.

leads.title: Han Kitab: Islam in Neo-Confucian terms
leads.summary: Chinese Muslim scholars such as Wang Daiyu and Liu Zhi expressed tawḥīd with Neo-Confucian metaphysics: 真一 'the Real One', li and qi, and the Supreme Ultimate, in dialogue with Zhu Xi.

passages.ref: Zhu Xi, commentaries; Zhou Dunyi, Taijitu shuo

leads.title: haykal: the Sumerian 'big house'
leads.summary: Sumerian é-gal ('big house', palace) became Akkadian ekallu, Hebrew hêkhāl (palace, temple), Aramaic hêkhlā, and Arabic haykal.

evidence.text: haykal does not occur in the Quran; it is a control case for the lexical track.

passages.text: כִּ֣י הַמַּגִּיד֩ לִ֨י לֵאמֹ֜ר הִנֵּה מֵ֣ת שָׁא֗וּל וְהֽוּא הָיָ֤ה כִמְבַשֵּׂר֙ בְּעֵינָ֔יו וָאֹחֲזָ֣ה ב֔וֹ וָאֶהְרְגֵ֖הוּ בְּצִֽקְלָ֑ג אֲשֶׁ֥ר לְתִתִּי ל֖וֹ בְּשֹׂרָֽה
וַיֹּ֧אמֶר ל֣וֹ יוֹאָ֗ב לֹא֩ אִ֨ישׁ בְּשֹׂרָ֤ה אַתָּה֙ הַיּ֣וֹם הַזֶּ֔ה וּבִשַּׂרְתָּ֖ בְּי֣וֹם אַחֵ֑ר וְהַיּ֤וֹם הַזֶּה֙ לֹ֣א תְבַשֵּׂ֔ר כִּֽי על עַל כֵּ֥ן בֶּן הַמֶּ֖לֶךְ מֵֽת

וַיֹּ֨סֶף ע֜וֹד אֲחִימַ֤עַץ בֶּן צָדוֹק֙ וַיֹּ֣אמֶר אֶל יוֹאָ֔ב וִ֣יהִי מָ֔ה אָרֻֽצָה נָּ֥א גַם אָ֖נִי אַחֲרֵ֣י הַכּוּשִׁ֑י וַיֹּ֣אמֶר יוֹאָ֗ב לָֽמָּה זֶּ֞ה אַתָּ֥ה רָץ֙ בְּנִ֔י וּלְכָ֖ה אֵין בְּשׂוֹרָ֥ה מֹצֵֽאת

וַיֹּ֣אמֶר הַמֶּ֔לֶךְ לַחֲכָמִ֖ים יֹדְעֵ֣י הָֽעִתִּ֑ים כִּי כֵן֙ דְּבַ֣ר הַמֶּ֔לֶךְ לִפְנֵ֕י כָּל יֹדְעֵ֖י דָּ֥ת וָדִֽין
כְּדָת֙ מַֽה לַּעֲשׂ֔וֹת בַּמַּלְכָּ֖ה וַשְׁתִּ֑י עַ֣ל אֲשֶׁ֣ר לֹֽא עָשְׂתָ֗ה אֶֽת מַאֲמַר֙ הַמֶּ֣לֶךְ אֲחַשְׁוֵר֔וֹשׁ בְּיַ֖ד הַסָּרִיסִֽים

אִם עַל הַמֶּ֣לֶךְ ט֗וֹב יֵצֵ֤א דְבַר מַלְכוּת֙ מִלְּפָנָ֔יו וְיִכָּתֵ֛ב בְּדָתֵ֥י פָֽרַס וּמָדַ֖י וְלֹ֣א יַעֲב֑וֹר אֲשֶׁ֨ר לֹֽא תָב֜וֹא וַשְׁתִּ֗י לִפְנֵי֙ הַמֶּ֣לֶךְ אֲחַשְׁוֵר֔וֹשׁ וּמַלְכוּתָהּ֙ יִתֵּ֣ן הַמֶּ֔לֶךְ לִרְעוּתָ֖הּ הַטּוֹבָ֥ה מִמֶּֽנָּה

וַיְהִ֗י בְּהִשָּׁמַ֤ע דְּבַר הַמֶּ֨לֶךְ֙ וְדָת֔וֹ וּֽבְהִקָּבֵ֞ץ נְעָר֥וֹת רַבּ֛וֹת אֶל שׁוּשַׁ֥ן הַבִּירָ֖ה אֶל יַ֣ד הֵגָ֑י וַתִּלָּקַ֤ח אֶסְתֵּר֙ אֶל בֵּ֣ית הַמֶּ֔לֶךְ אֶל יַ֥ד הֵגַ֖י שֹׁמֵ֥ר הַנָּשִֽׁים

וּבְהַגִּ֡יעַ תֹּר֩ נַעֲרָ֨ה וְנַעֲרָ֜ה לָב֣וֹא אֶל הַמֶּ֣לֶךְ אֲחַשְׁוֵר֗וֹשׁ מִקֵּץ֩ הֱי֨וֹת לָ֜הּ כְּדָ֤ת הַנָּשִׁים֙ שְׁנֵ֣ים עָשָׂ֣ר חֹ֔דֶשׁ כִּ֛י כֵּ֥ן יִמְלְא֖וּ יְמֵ֣י מְרוּקֵיהֶ֑ן שִׁשָּׁ֤ה חֳדָשִׁים֙ בְּשֶׁ֣מֶן הַמֹּ֔ר וְשִׁשָּׁ֤ה חֳדָשִׁים֙ בַּבְּשָׂמִ֔ים וּבְתַמְרוּקֵ֖י הַנָּשִֽׁים

וַיֹּ֤אמֶר הָמָן֙ לַמֶּ֣לֶךְ אֲחַשְׁוֵר֔וֹשׁ יֶשְׁנ֣וֹ עַם אֶחָ֗ד מְפֻזָּ֤ר וּמְפֹרָד֙ בֵּ֣ין הָֽעַמִּ֔ים בְּכֹ֖ל מְדִינ֣וֹת מַלְכוּתֶ֑ךָ וְדָתֵיהֶ֞ם שֹׁנ֣וֹת מִכָּל עָ֗ם וְאֶת דָּתֵ֤י הַמֶּ֨לֶךְ֙ אֵינָ֣ם עֹשִׂ֔ים וְלַמֶּ֥לֶךְ אֵין שֹׁוֶ֖ה לְהַנִּיחָֽם
פַּתְשֶׁ֣גֶן הַכְּתָ֗ב לְהִנָּ֤תֵֽן דָּת֙ בְּכָל מְדִינָ֣ה וּמְדִינָ֔ה גָּל֖וּי לְכָל הָֽעַמִּ֑ים לִהְי֥וֹת עֲתִדִ֖ים לַיּ֥וֹם הַזֶּֽה
הָֽרָצִ֞ים יָצְא֤וּ דְחוּפִים֙ בִּדְבַ֣ר הַמֶּ֔לֶךְ וְהַדָּ֥ת נִתְּנָ֖ה בְּשׁוּשַׁ֣ן הַבִּירָ֑ה וְהַמֶּ֤לֶךְ וְהָמָן֙ יָשְׁב֣וּ לִשְׁתּ֔וֹת וְהָעִ֥יר שׁוּשָׁ֖ן נָבֽוֹכָה
וּבְכָל מְדִינָ֣ה וּמְדִינָ֗ה מְקוֹם֙ אֲשֶׁ֨ר דְּבַר הַמֶּ֤לֶךְ וְדָתוֹ֙ מַגִּ֔יעַ אֵ֤בֶל גָּדוֹל֙ לַיְּהוּדִ֔ים וְצ֥וֹם וּבְכִ֖י וּמִסְפֵּ֑ד שַׂ֣ק וָאֵ֔פֶר יֻצַּ֖ע לָֽרַבִּֽים

וְאֶת פַּתְשֶׁ֣גֶן כְּתָֽב הַ֠דָּת אֲשֶׁר נִתַּ֨ן בְּשׁוּשָׁ֤ן לְהַשְׁמִידָם֙ נָ֣תַן ל֔וֹ לְהַרְא֥וֹת אֶת אֶסְתֵּ֖ר וּלְהַגִּ֣יד לָ֑הּ וּלְצַוּ֣וֹת עָלֶ֗יהָ לָב֨וֹא אֶל הַמֶּ֧לֶךְ לְהִֽתְחַנֶּן ל֛וֹ וּלְבַקֵּ֥שׁ מִלְּפָנָ֖יו עַל עַמָּֽהּ

כָּל עַבְדֵ֣י הַמֶּ֡לֶךְ וְעַם מְדִינ֨וֹת הַמֶּ֜לֶךְ יֽוֹדְעִ֗ים אֲשֶׁ֣ר כָּל אִ֣ישׁ וְאִשָּׁ֡ה אֲשֶׁ֣ר יָבֽוֹא אֶל הַמֶּלֶךְ֩ אֶל הֶחָצֵ֨ר הַפְּנִימִ֜ית אֲשֶׁ֣ר לֹֽא יִקָּרֵ֗א אַחַ֤ת דָּתוֹ֙ לְהָמִ֔ית לְ֠בַד מֵאֲשֶׁ֨ר יֽוֹשִׁיט ל֥וֹ הַמֶּ֛לֶךְ אֶת שַׁרְבִ֥יט הַזָּהָ֖ב וְחָיָ֑ה וַאֲנִ֗י לֹ֤א נִקְרֵ֨אתי֙ לָב֣וֹא אֶל הַמֶּ֔לֶךְ זֶ֖ה שְׁלוֹשִׁ֥ים יֽוֹם

לֵךְ֩ כְּנ֨וֹס אֶת כָּל הַיְּהוּדִ֜ים הַֽנִּמְצְאִ֣ים בְּשׁוּשָׁ֗ן וְצ֣וּמוּ עָ֠לַי וְאַל תֹּאכְל֨וּ וְאַל תִּשְׁתּ֜וּ שְׁלֹ֤שֶׁת יָמִים֙ לַ֣יְלָה וָי֔וֹם גַּם אֲנִ֥י וְנַעֲרֹתַ֖י אָצ֣וּם כֵּ֑ן וּבְכֵ֞ן אָב֤וֹא אֶל הַמֶּ֨לֶךְ֙ אֲשֶׁ֣ר לֹֽא כַדָּ֔ת וְכַאֲשֶׁ֥ר אָבַ֖דְתִּי אָבָֽדְתִּי

leads.title: malkâh: a word shared by Esther and Solomon
leads.summary: מַלְכָּה (malkâh, H4436) occurs in 34 verses, all or nearly all inside two narratives: Esther (24) and Solomon (8). A rare word linking two stories.

passages.text: וּמַֽלְכַּת שְׁבָ֗א שֹׁמַ֛עַת אֶת שֵׁ֥מַע שְׁלֹמֹ֖ה לְשֵׁ֣ם יְהוָ֑ה וַתָּבֹ֥א לְנַסֹּת֖וֹ בְּחִידֽוֹת
וַתֵּ֨רֶא֙ מַֽלְכַּת שְׁבָ֔א אֵ֖ת כָּל חָכְמַ֣ת שְׁלֹמֹ֑ה וְהַבַּ֖יִת אֲשֶׁ֥ר בָּנָֽה

וַתִּתֵּ֨ן לַמֶּ֜לֶךְ מֵאָ֥ה וְעֶשְׂרִ֣ים כִּכַּ֣ר זָהָ֗ב וּבְשָׂמִ֛ים הַרְבֵּ֥ה מְאֹ֖ד וְאֶ֣בֶן יְקָרָ֑ה לֹא בָא֩ כַבֹּ֨שֶׂם הַה֥וּא עוֹד֙ לָרֹ֔ב אֲשֶׁר נָתְנָ֥ה מַֽלְכַּת שְׁבָ֖א לַמֶּ֥לֶךְ שְׁלֹמֹֽה
וְהַמֶּ֨לֶךְ שְׁלֹמֹ֜ה נָתַ֣ן לְמַֽלְכַּת שְׁבָ֗א אֶת כָּל חֶפְצָהּ֙ אֲשֶׁ֣ר שָׁאָ֔לָה מִלְּבַד֙ אֲשֶׁ֣ר נָֽתַן לָ֔הּ כְּיַ֖ד הַמֶּ֣לֶךְ שְׁלֹמֹ֑ה וַתֵּ֛פֶן וַתֵּ֥לֶךְ לְאַרְצָ֖הּ הִ֥יא וַעֲבָדֶֽיהָ

וּמַֽלְכַּת שְׁבָ֗א שָֽׁמְעָה֮ אֶת שֵׁ֣מַע שְׁלֹמֹה֒ וַתָּב֣וֹא לְנַסּוֹת֩ אֶת שְׁלֹמֹ֨ה בְחִיד֜וֹת בִּירֽוּשָׁלִַ֗ם בְּחַ֣יִל כָּבֵ֣ד מְאֹ֡ד וּ֠גְמַלִּים נֹשְׂאִ֨ים בְּשָׂמִ֧ים וְזָהָ֛ב לָרֹ֖ב וְאֶ֣בֶן יְקָרָ֑ה וַתָּבוֹא֙ אֶל שְׁלֹמֹ֔ה וַתְּדַבֵּ֣ר עִמּ֔וֹ אֵ֛ת כָּל אֲשֶׁ֥ר הָיָ֖ה עִם לְבָבָֽהּ
וַתֵּ֨רֶא֙ מַֽלְכַּת שְׁבָ֔א אֵ֖ת חָכְמַ֣ת שְׁלֹמֹ֑ה וְהַבַּ֖יִת אֲשֶׁ֥ר בָּנָֽה
וַתִּתֵּ֨ן לַמֶּ֜לֶךְ מֵאָ֥ה וְעֶשְׂרִ֣ים כִּכַּ֣ר זָהָ֗ב וּבְשָׂמִ֛ים לָרֹ֥ב מְאֹ֖ד וְאֶ֣בֶן יְקָרָ֑ה וְלֹ֤א הָיָה֙ כַּבֹּ֣שֶׂם הַה֔וּא אֲשֶׁר נָתְנָ֥ה מַֽלְכַּת שְׁבָ֖א לַמֶּ֥לֶךְ שְׁלֹמֹֽה
וְהַמֶּ֨לֶךְ שְׁלֹמֹ֜ה נָתַ֣ן לְמַֽלְכַּת שְׁבָ֗א אֶת כָּל חֶפְצָהּ֙ אֲשֶׁ֣ר שָׁאָ֔לָה מִלְּבַ֖ד אֲשֶׁר הֵבִ֣יאָה אֶל הַמֶּ֑לֶךְ וַֽתַּהֲפֹ֛ךְ וַתֵּ֥לֶךְ לְאַרְצָ֖הּ הִ֥יא וַעֲבָדֶֽיהָ
גַּ֚ם וַשְׁתִּ֣י הַמַּלְכָּ֔ה עָשְׂתָ֖ה מִשְׁתֵּ֣ה נָשִׁ֑ים בֵּ֚ית הַמַּלְכ֔וּת אֲשֶׁ֖ר לַמֶּ֥לֶךְ אֲחַשְׁוֵרֽוֹשׁ
לְ֠הָבִיא אֶת וַשְׁתִּ֧י הַמַּלְכָּ֛ה לִפְנֵ֥י הַמֶּ֖לֶךְ בְּכֶ֣תֶר מַלְכ֑וּת לְהַרְא֨וֹת הָֽעַמִּ֤ים וְהַשָּׂרִים֙ אֶת יָפְיָ֔הּ כִּֽי טוֹבַ֥ת מַרְאֶ֖ה הִֽיא
וַתְּמָאֵ֞ן הַמַּלְכָּ֣ה וַשְׁתִּ֗י לָבוֹא֙ בִּדְבַ֣ר הַמֶּ֔לֶךְ אֲשֶׁ֖ר בְּיַ֣ד הַסָּרִיסִ֑ים וַיִּקְצֹ֤ף הַמֶּ֨לֶךְ֙ מְאֹ֔ד וַחֲמָת֖וֹ בָּעֲרָ֥ה בֽוֹ
כְּדָת֙ מַֽה לַּעֲשׂ֔וֹת בַּמַּלְכָּ֖ה וַשְׁתִּ֑י עַ֣ל אֲשֶׁ֣ר לֹֽא עָשְׂתָ֗ה אֶֽת מַאֲמַר֙ הַמֶּ֣לֶךְ אֲחַשְׁוֵר֔וֹשׁ בְּיַ֖ד הַסָּרִיסִֽים

וַיֹּ֣אמֶר מומכן מְמוּכָ֗ן לִפְנֵ֤י הַמֶּ֨לֶךְ֙ וְהַשָּׂרִ֔ים לֹ֤א עַל הַמֶּ֨לֶךְ֙ לְבַדּ֔וֹ עָוְתָ֖ה וַשְׁתִּ֣י הַמַּלְכָּ֑ה כִּ֤י עַל כָּל הַשָּׂרִים֙ וְעַל כָּל הָ֣עַמִּ֔ים אֲשֶׁ֕ר בְּכָל מְדִינ֖וֹת הַמֶּ֥לֶךְ אֲחַשְׁוֵרֽוֹשׁ
כִּֽי יֵצֵ֤א דְבַר הַמַּלְכָּה֙ עַל כָּל הַנָּשִׁ֔ים לְהַבְז֥וֹת בַּעְלֵיהֶ֖ן בְּעֵינֵיהֶ֑ן בְּאָמְרָ֗ם הַמֶּ֣לֶךְ אֲחַשְׁוֵר֡וֹשׁ אָמַ֞ר לְהָבִ֨יא אֶת וַשְׁתִּ֧י הַמַּלְכָּ֛ה לְפָנָ֖יו וְלֹא בָֽאָה
וְֽהַיּ֨וֹם הַזֶּ֜ה תֹּאמַ֣רְנָה שָׂר֣וֹת פָּֽרַס וּמָדַ֗י אֲשֶׁ֤ר שָֽׁמְעוּ֙ אֶת דְּבַ֣ר הַמַּלְכָּ֔ה לְכֹ֖ל שָׂרֵ֣י הַמֶּ֑לֶךְ וּכְדַ֖י בִּזָּי֥וֹן וָקָֽצֶף

leads.title: millâh: a word shared by David and Job
leads.summary: מִלָּה (millâh, H4405) occurs in 38 verses, all or nearly all inside two narratives: David (1) and Job (34). A rare word linking two stories.

passages.text: ר֥וּחַ יְהוָ֖ה דִּבֶּר בִּ֑י וּמִלָּת֖וֹ עַל לְשׁוֹנִֽי
הֲנִסָּ֬ה דָבָ֣ר אֵלֶ֣יךָ תִּלְאֶ֑ה וַעְצֹ֥ר בְּ֝מִלִּ֗ין מִ֣י יוּכָֽל
כּ֭וֹשֵׁל יְקִימ֣וּן מִלֶּ֑יךָ וּבִרְכַּ֖יִם כֹּרְע֣וֹת תְּאַמֵּֽץ
הַלְהוֹכַ֣ח מִלִּ֣ים תַּחְשֹׁ֑בוּ וּ֝לְר֗וּחַ אִמְרֵ֥י נֹאָֽשׁ
הֲלֹא הֵ֣ם י֭וֹרוּךָ יֹ֣אמְרוּ לָ֑ךְ וּ֝מִלִּבָּ֗ם יוֹצִ֥אוּ מִלִּֽים
הֲלֹא אֹ֭זֶן מִלִּ֣ין תִּבְחָ֑ן וְ֝חֵ֗ךְ אֹ֣כֶל יִטְעַם לֽוֹ

וְזֶ֕ה אֲשֶׁ֥ר תַּֽעֲשֶׂ֖ה אֹתָ֑הּ שְׁלֹ֧שׁ מֵא֣וֹת אַמָּ֗ה אֹ֚רֶךְ הַתֵּבָ֔ה חֲמִשִּׁ֤ים אַמָּה֙ רָחְבָּ֔הּ וּשְׁלֹשִׁ֥ים אַמָּ֖ה קוֹמָתָֽהּ
צֹ֣הַר תַּֽעֲשֶׂ֣ה לַתֵּבָ֗ה וְאֶל אַמָּה֙ תְּכַלֶ֣נָּה מִלְמַ֔עְלָה וּפֶ֥תַח הַתֵּבָ֖ה בְּצִדָּ֣הּ תָּשִׂ֑ים תַּחְתִּיִּ֛ם שְׁנִיִּ֥ם וּשְׁלִשִׁ֖ים תַּֽעֲשֶֽׂהָ

וּמִכָּל הָ֠חַי מִֽכָּל בָּשָׂ֞ר שְׁנַ֧יִם מִכֹּ֛ל תָּבִ֥יא אֶל הַתֵּבָ֖ה לְהַחֲיֹ֣ת אִתָּ֑ךְ זָכָ֥ר וּנְקֵבָ֖ה יִֽהְיֽוּ
וַיֹּ֤אמֶר יְהוָה֙ לְנֹ֔חַ בֹּֽא אַתָּ֥ה וְכָל בֵּיתְךָ֖ אֶל הַתֵּבָ֑ה כִּֽי אֹתְךָ֥ רָאִ֛יתִי צַדִּ֥יק לְפָנַ֖י בַּדּ֥וֹר הַזֶּֽה
וַיָּ֣בֹא נֹ֗חַ וּ֠בָנָיו וְאִשְׁתּ֧וֹ וּנְשֵֽׁי בָנָ֛יו אִתּ֖וֹ אֶל הַתֵּבָ֑ה מִפְּנֵ֖י מֵ֥י הַמַּבּֽוּל
שְׁנַ֨יִם שְׁנַ֜יִם בָּ֧אוּ אֶל נֹ֛חַ אֶל הַתֵּבָ֖ה זָכָ֣ר וּנְקֵבָ֑ה כַּֽאֲשֶׁ֛ר צִוָּ֥ה אֱלֹהִ֖ים אֶת נֹֽחַ

וַיָּבֹ֥אוּ אֶל נֹ֖חַ אֶל הַתֵּבָ֑ה שְׁנַ֤יִם שְׁנַ֨יִם֙ מִכָּל הַבָּשָׂ֔ר אֲשֶׁר בּ֖וֹ ר֥וּחַ חַיִּֽים
וַֽיְהִ֧י הַמַּבּ֛וּל אַרְבָּעִ֥ים י֖וֹם עַל הָאָ֑רֶץ וַיִּרְבּ֣וּ הַמַּ֗יִם וַיִּשְׂאוּ֙ אֶת הַתֵּבָ֔ה וַתָּ֖רָם מֵעַ֥ל הָאָֽרֶץ

וַיִּ֜מַח אֶֽת כָּל הַיְק֣וּם אֲשֶׁ֣ר עַל פְּנֵ֣י הָֽאֲדָמָ֗ה מֵאָדָ֤ם עַד בְּהֵמָה֙ עַד רֶ֨מֶשׂ֙ וְעַד ע֣וֹף הַשָּׁמַ֔יִם וַיִּמָּח֖וּ מִן הָאָ֑רֶץ וַיִשָּׁ֧אֶר אַךְ נֹ֛חַ וַֽאֲשֶׁ֥ר אִתּ֖וֹ בַּתֵּבָֽה

passages.text: וַיֹּאמְר֣וּ אֵלָ֔יו חֲל֣וֹם חָלַ֔מְנוּ וּפֹתֵ֖ר אֵ֣ין אֹת֑וֹ וַיֹּ֨אמֶר אֲלֵהֶ֜ם יוֹסֵ֗ף הֲל֤וֹא לֵֽאלֹהִים֙ פִּתְרֹנִ֔ים סַפְּרוּ נָ֖א לִֽי
וַיַּ֥רְא שַׂר הָאֹפִ֖ים כִּ֣י ט֣וֹב פָּתָ֑ר וַיֹּ֨אמֶר֙ אֶל יוֹסֵ֔ף אַף אֲנִי֙ בַּחֲלוֹמִ֔י וְהִנֵּ֗ה שְׁלֹשָׁ֛ה סַלֵּ֥י חֹרִ֖י עַל רֹאשִֽׁי
וְאֵ֛ת שַׂ֥ר הָאֹפִ֖ים תָּלָ֑ה כַּאֲשֶׁ֥ר פָּתַ֛ר לָהֶ֖ם יוֹסֵֽף
וַיְהִ֤י בַבֹּ֨קֶר֙ וַתִּפָּ֣עֶם רוּח֔וֹ וַיִּשְׁלַ֗ח וַיִּקְרָ֛א אֶת כָּל חַרְטֻמֵּ֥י מִצְרַ֖יִם וְאֶת כָּל חֲכָמֶ֑יהָ וַיְסַפֵּ֨ר פַּרְעֹ֤ה לָהֶם֙ אֶת חֲלֹמ֔וֹ וְאֵין פּוֹתֵ֥ר אוֹתָ֖ם לְפַרְעֹֽה
וְשָׁ֨ם אִתָּ֜נוּ נַ֣עַר עִבְרִ֗י עֶ֚בֶד לְשַׂ֣ר הַטַּבָּחִ֔ים וַנְּ֨סַפֶּר ל֔וֹ וַיִּפְתָּר לָ֖נוּ אֶת חֲלֹמֹתֵ֑ינוּ אִ֥ישׁ כַּחֲלֹמ֖וֹ פָּתָֽר
וַיְהִ֛י כַּאֲשֶׁ֥ר פָּֽתַר לָ֖נוּ כֵּ֣ן הָיָ֑ה אֹתִ֛י הֵשִׁ֥יב עַל כַּנִּ֖י וְאֹת֥וֹ תָלָֽה
וַיֹּ֤אמֶר פַּרְעֹה֙ אֶל יוֹסֵ֔ף חֲל֣וֹם חָלַ֔מְתִּי וּפֹתֵ֖ר אֵ֣ין אֹת֑וֹ וַאֲנִ֗י שָׁמַ֤עְתִּי עָלֶ֨יךָ֙ לֵאמֹ֔ר תִּשְׁמַ֥ע חֲל֖וֹם לִפְתֹּ֥ר אֹתֽוֹ

passages.text: אֶת הַמְּנֹרָ֨ה הַטְּהֹרָ֜ה אֶת נֵרֹתֶ֗יהָ נֵרֹ֛ת הַמַּֽעֲרָכָ֖ה וְאֶת כָּל כֵּלֶ֑יהָ וְאֵ֖ת שֶׁ֥מֶן הַמָּאֽוֹר
וְשַׂמְתָּ֥ אוֹתָ֛ם שְׁתַּ֥יִם מַֽעֲרָכ֖וֹת שֵׁ֣שׁ הַֽמַּעֲרָ֑כֶת עַ֛ל הַשֻּׁלְחָ֥ן הַטָּהֹ֖ר לִפְנֵ֥י יְהוָֽה
וּבָנִ֨יתָ מִזְבֵּ֜חַ לַיהוָ֣ה אֱלֹהֶ֗יךָ עַ֣ל רֹ֧אשׁ הַמָּע֛וֹז הַזֶּ֖ה בַּמַּֽעֲרָכָ֑ה וְלָֽקַחְתָּ֙ אֶת הַפָּ֣ר הַשֵּׁנִ֔י וְהַעֲלִ֣יתָ עוֹלָ֔ה בַּעֲצֵ֥י הָאֲשֵׁרָ֖ה אֲשֶׁ֥ר תִּכְרֹֽת
וַיַּעַרְכ֨וּ פְלִשְׁתִּ֜ים לִקְרַ֣את יִשְׂרָאֵ֗ל וַתִּטֹּשׁ֙ הַמִּלְחָמָ֔ה וַיִּנָּ֥גֶף יִשְׂרָאֵ֖ל לִפְנֵ֣י פְלִשְׁתִּ֑ים וַיַּכּ֤וּ בַמַּֽעֲרָכָה֙ בַּשָּׂדֶ֔ה כְּאַרְבַּ֥עַת אֲלָפִ֖ים אִֽישׁ
וַיָּ֤רָץ אִישׁ בִּנְיָמִן֙ מֵהַמַּ֣עֲרָכָ֔ה וַיָּבֹ֥א שִׁלֹ֖ה בַּיּ֣וֹם הַה֑וּא וּמַדָּ֣יו קְרֻעִ֔ים וַאֲדָמָ֖ה עַל רֹאשֽׁוֹ
וַיֹּ֨אמֶר הָאִ֜ישׁ אֶל עֵלִ֗י אָֽנֹכִי֙ הַבָּ֣א מִן הַמַּעֲרָכָ֔ה וַאֲנִ֕י מִן הַמַּעֲרָכָ֖ה נַ֣סְתִּי הַיּ֑וֹם וַיֹּ֛אמֶר מֶֽה הָיָ֥ה הַדָּבָ֖ר בְּנִֽי

וַֽיַּעֲמֹ֗ד וַיִּקְרָא֙ אֶל מַעַרְכֹ֣ת יִשְׂרָאֵ֔ל וַיֹּ֣אמֶר לָהֶ֔ם לָ֥מָּה תֵצְא֖וּ לַעֲרֹ֣ךְ מִלְחָמָ֑ה הֲל֧וֹא אָנֹכִ֣י הַפְּלִשְׁתִּ֗י וְאַתֶּם֙ עֲבָדִ֣ים לְשָׁא֔וּל בְּרוּ לָכֶ֥ם אִ֖ישׁ וְיֵרֵ֥ד אֵלָֽי
וַיֹּ֨אמֶר֙ הַפְּלִשְׁתִּ֔י אֲנִ֗י חֵרַ֛פְתִּי אֶת מַעַרְכ֥וֹת יִשְׂרָאֵ֖ל הַיּ֣וֹם הַזֶּ֑ה תְּנוּ לִ֣י אִ֔ישׁ וְנִֽלָּחֲמָ֖ה יָֽחַד

וַיַּשְׁכֵּ֨ם דָּוִ֜ד בַּבֹּ֗קֶר וַיִּטֹּ֤שׁ אֶת הַצֹּאן֙ עַל שֹׁמֵ֔ר וַיִּשָּׂ֣א וַיֵּ֔לֶךְ כַּאֲשֶׁ֥ר צִוָּ֖הוּ יִשָׁ֑י וַיָּבֹא֙ הַמַּעְגָּ֔לָה וְהַחַ֗יִל הַיֹּצֵא֙ אֶל הַמַּ֣עֲרָכָ֔ה וְהֵרֵ֖עוּ בַּמִּלְחָמָֽה
וַתַּעֲרֹ֤ךְ יִשְׂרָאֵל֙ וּפְלִשְׁתִּ֔ים מַעֲרָכָ֖ה לִקְרַ֥את מַעֲרָכָֽה
וַיִּטֹּשׁ֩ דָּוִ֨ד אֶת הַכֵּלִ֜ים מֵעָלָ֗יו עַל יַד֙ שׁוֹמֵ֣ר הַכֵּלִ֔ים וַיָּ֖רָץ הַמַּעֲרָכָ֑ה וַיָּבֹ֕א וַיִּשְׁאַ֥ל לְאֶחָ֖יו לְשָׁלֽוֹם
וְה֣וּא מְדַבֵּ֣ר עִמָּ֗ם וְהִנֵּ֣ה אִ֣ישׁ הַבֵּנַ֡יִם עוֹלֶ֞ה גָּלְיָת֩ הַפְּלִשְׁתִּ֨י שְׁמ֤וֹ מִגַּת֙ ממערות מִמַּעַרְכ֣וֹת פְּלִשְׁתִּ֔ים וַיְדַבֵּ֖ר כַּדְּבָרִ֣ים הָאֵ֑לֶּה וַיִּשְׁמַ֖ע דָּוִֽד

וַיֹּ֣אמֶר דָּוִ֗ד אֶֽל הָאֲנָשִׁ֞ים הָעֹמְדִ֣ים עִמּוֹ֮ לֵאמֹר֒ מַה יֵּעָשֶׂ֗ה לָאִישׁ֙ אֲשֶׁ֤ר יַכֶּה֙ אֶת הַפְּלִשְׁתִּ֣י הַלָּ֔ז וְהֵסִ֥יר חֶרְפָּ֖ה מֵעַ֣ל יִשְׂרָאֵ֑ל כִּ֣י מִ֗י הַפְּלִשְׁתִּ֤י הֶֽעָרֵל֙ הַזֶּ֔ה כִּ֣י חֵרֵ֔ף מַעַרְכ֖וֹת אֱלֹהִ֥ים חַיִּֽים
גַּ֧ם אֶֽת הָאֲרִ֛י גַּם הַדּ֖וֹב הִכָּ֣ה עַבְדֶּ֑ךָ וְֽ֠הָיָה הַפְּלִשְׁתִּ֨י הֶעָרֵ֤ל הַזֶּה֙ כְּאַחַ֣ד מֵהֶ֔ם כִּ֣י חֵרֵ֔ף מַעַרְכֹ֖ת אֱלֹהִ֥ים חַיִּֽים
וַיֹּ֤אמֶר דָּוִד֙ אֶל הַפְּלִשְׁתִּ֔י אַתָּה֙ בָּ֣א אֵלַ֔י בְּחֶ֖רֶב וּבַחֲנִ֣ית וּבְכִיד֑וֹן וְאָנֹכִ֣י בָֽא אֵלֶ֗יךָ בְּשֵׁם֙ יְהוָ֣ה צְבָא֔וֹת אֱלֹהֵ֛י מַעַרְכ֥וֹת יִשְׂרָאֵ֖ל אֲשֶׁ֥ר חֵרַֽפְתָּ

leads.title: Satan refuses to bow to Adam
leads.summary: God commands the angels to honor Adam, and Satan refuses. Found in the Life of Adam and Eve and the Cave of Treasures, and repeatedly in the Quran.

passages.ref: Life of Adam and Eve (Latin Vita 12–16)

leads.title: The Kalam cosmological argument
leads.summary: The argument that the universe began and so has a cause, developed by the mutakallimūn and al-Ghazali, was revived and named by William Lane Craig in analytic philosophy of religion.

passages.ref: W. L. Craig, The Kalām Cosmological Argument (1979)

leads.title: Panchatantra to Kalila wa-Dimna
leads.summary: The Sanskrit Panchatantra was translated into Middle Persian (Burzoy, 6th c.), then Arabic (Ibn al-Muqaffaʿ, 8th c.), then into Hebrew, Greek, Latin, and most European languages.

leads.title: Kumarbi cycle and Hesiod's Theogony
leads.summary: Both have the same succession myth: Anu, Kumarbi, Teshub in the Hurro-Hittite cycle and Ouranos, Kronos, Zeus in Hesiod, including a sky god castrated by his successor.

leads.title: kursī: Sumerian throne to Quranic seat
leads.summary: Sumerian guza passed into Akkadian kussû, Aramaic kursēʾ, and Arabic kursī. The Quran's Throne Verse (2:255) uses it.

passages.note: His kursī encompasses the heavens and the earth
passages.text: ٱللَّهُ لَآ إِلَٰهَ إِلَّا هُوَ ٱلْحَىُّ ٱلْقَيُّومُ لَا تَأْخُذُهُۥ سِنَةٌ وَلَا نَوْمٌ لَّهُۥ مَا فِى ٱلسَّمَٰوَٰتِ وَمَا فِى ٱلْأَرْضِ مَن ذَا ٱلَّذِى يَشْفَعُ عِندَهُۥٓ إِلَّا بِإِذْنِهِۦ يَعْلَمُ مَا بَيْنَ أَيْدِيهِمْ وَمَا خَلْفَهُمْ وَلَا يُحِيطُونَ بِشَىْءٍ مِّنْ عِلْمِهِۦٓ إِلَّا بِمَا شَآءَ وَسِعَ كُرْسِيُّهُ ٱلسَّمَٰوَٰتِ وَٱلْأَرْضَ وَلَا يَـُٔودُهُۥ حِفْظُهُمَا وَهُوَ ٱلْعَلِىُّ ٱلْعَظِيمُ

passages.note: Solomon's kursī
passages.text: وَلَقَدْ فَتَنَّا سُلَيْمَٰنَ وَأَلْقَيْنَا عَلَىٰ كُرْسِيِّهِۦ جَسَدًا ثُمَّ أَنَابَ

evidence.text: Arabic kursī shows the Aramaic -r- form (dissimilated -ss- > -rs-), which points to Aramaic as the immediate source.

leads.title: Mani and the 'seal of the prophets'
leads.summary: Quran 33:40 calls Muhammad khātam al-nabiyyīn. Manichaean sources present Mani as the last in a line of prophets (Buddha, Zoroaster, Jesus), and whether 'seal' was a Manichaean title is debated.

passages.text: مَّا كَانَ مُحَمَّدٌ أَبَآ أَحَدٍ مِّن رِّجَالِكُمْ وَلَٰكِن رَّسُولَ ٱللَّهِ وَخَاتَمَ ٱلنَّبِيِّۦنَ وَكَانَ ٱللَّهُ بِكُلِّ شَىْءٍ عَلِيمًا

passages.ref: Kephalaia 1; al-Biruni's quotation of the Shābuhragān

evidence.text: See Stroumsa, 'Seal of the Prophets: The Nature of a Manichaean Metaphor' (1986), for the case against reading it as a Manichaean title.

leads.title: Mary raised in the Temple
leads.summary: The Protevangelium of James has Mary dedicated to the Temple, fed by an angel, and her guardian chosen by a sign. The Quran has Mary's dedication, miraculous provision in the sanctuary, Zechariah as guardian, and lots cast for her care.

passages.text: (3:35) إِذْ قَالَتِ ٱمْرَأَتُ عِمْرَٰنَ رَبِّ إِنِّى نَذَرْتُ لَكَ مَا فِى بَطْنِى مُحَرَّرًا فَتَقَبَّلْ مِنِّىٓ إِنَّكَ أَنتَ ٱلسَّمِيعُ ٱلْعَلِيمُ (3:36) فَلَمَّا وَضَعَتْهَا قَالَتْ رَبِّ إِنِّى وَضَعْتُهَآ أُنثَىٰ وَٱللَّهُ أَعْلَمُ بِمَا وَضَعَتْ وَلَيْسَ ٱلذَّكَرُ كَٱلْأُنثَىٰ وَإِنِّى سَمَّيْتُهَا مَرْيَمَ وَإِنِّىٓ أُعِيذُهَا بِكَ وَذُرِّيَّتَهَا مِنَ ٱلشَّيْطَٰنِ ٱلرَّجِيمِ (3:37) فَتَقَبَّلَهَا رَبُّهَا بِقَبُولٍ حَسَنٍ وَأَنۢبَتَهَا نَبَاتًا حَسَنًا وَكَفَّلَهَا زَكَرِيَّا كُلَّمَا دَخَلَ عَلَيْهَا زَكَرِيَّا ٱلْمِحْرَابَ وَجَدَ عِندَهَا رِزْقًا قَالَ يَٰمَرْيَمُ أَنَّىٰ لَكِ هَٰذَا قَالَتْ هُوَ مِنْ عِندِ ٱللَّهِ إِنَّ ٱللَّهَ يَرْزُقُ مَن يَشَآءُ بِغَيْرِ حِسَابٍ (3:44) ذَٰلِكَ مِنْ أَنۢبَآءِ ٱلْغَيْبِ نُوحِيهِ إِلَيْكَ وَمَا كُنتَ لَدَيْهِمْ إِذْ يُلْقُونَ أَقْلَٰمَهُمْ أَيُّهُمْ يَكْفُلُ مَرْيَمَ وَمَا كُنتَ لَدَيْهِمْ إِذْ يَخْتَصِمُونَ

leads.title: Mary and the palm tree
leads.summary: In Pseudo-Matthew a palm bends to feed Mary and a spring opens during the flight to Egypt. In the Quran a palm and a stream sustain Mary during the birth of Jesus.

leads.title: Atrahasis: the flood (Middle Babylonian fragments, the boat and the birds) ↔ The Flood (full read)
leads.summary: 7 shared motifs, found by the separate reads; not yet compared side by side.

evidence.text: Shared motifs, rarest first: Birds released to find dry land (weight 6.6); Exact dimensions of the vessel are specified (weight 6.5); Animals taken aboard in pairs (weight 6.5); Vessel has several decks, a side door and a roof opening or window (weight 6.2); Vessel sealed with pitch or bitumen (weight 6.2); Hero privately warned of the coming flood by a deity (weight 5.8); Hero's family saved with him (weight 5.4). Pair score 43.4.

Only in Atrahasis: the flood (Middle Babylonian fragments, the boat and the birds): The flood hero is told: 'Destroy your house, build a boat; spurn property, save life'; Once the hero has entered the boat its door is sealed shut; A dove released from the boat flies off and returns because she has exhausted her wings and found no place; From his throne the high god takes an oath to annihilate (humankind) totally; While those boarding eat and drink, the flood hero alone is heavy-hearted, knowing what is coming; The flood boat is to be built on a circular plan, its length equal to its breadth, like a giant coracle; A god appears to a man in a dream and gives him practical instructions, which he carries out; Warning spoken to a wall or reed hut so the hero overhears.

Only in The Flood (full read): Clean animals taken aboard by sevens, unclean by pairs; Flood events given exact calendar dates (year of hero's life, month, day); Rain or flood lasts forty days and forty nights; A dove returns with an olive leaf in its beak; Seven days pass between the warning or boarding and the onset of the flood; Angels object that the new human will corrupt the earth and shed blood while they praise God; When the water overflowed God carried 'you' in the running ship (al-jariya) as a reminder for retaining ears [divergence between the texts]; What sets the flood in motion: God's decision on violence, or the rejected prophet's prayer [divergence between the texts]; How the ark is described [divergence between the texts]; What the flood hero does when the vessel comes to rest [divergence between the texts]; What God says of later generations after the flood: no repeat, or punishment to come [contrast between the texts]; How the flood waters are stopped and subside [divergence between the texts]; and 39 more.

leads.summary: 20 shared motifs, found by the separate reads; not yet compared side by side.

evidence.text: Shared motifs, rarest first: God regrets having made humankind and is grieved in his heart (weight 7.3); A raven is sent out and does not return (goes to and fro) (weight 7.3); God sends a wind (ruah) over the earth to make the waters subside (weight 7.3); God himself shuts the vessel's door behind the hero (weight 7.3); What the flood hero does when the vessel comes to rest (weight 7.1); Whether the flood hero speaks to his people before the flood (weight 6.8); Deity resolves or promises not to repeat the destruction (weight 6.6); Birds released to find dry land (weight 6.6); Deity or gods smell the offering (weight 6.5); Exact dimensions of the vessel are specified (weight 6.5); Vessel comes to rest on a named mountain (weight 6.4); Waters pour both from the sky and from springs of the earth (weight 6.2); Vessel has several decks, a side door and a roof opening or window (weight 6.2); Vessel sealed with pitch or bitumen (weight 6.2); Hero offers sacrifice after leaving the vessel (weight 6.2); Hero builds a vessel on divine instruction (weight 6.2); Deity decides to destroy humankind (weight 6.1); All others perish (weight 5.9); Hero privately warned of the coming flood by a deity (weight 5.8); Hero's family saved with him (weight 5.4). Pair score 130.3.

Only in Utnapishtim's flood (Gilgamesh, Standard Babylonian Tablet XI:8-206): The divine warning commands: abandon riches, spurn property and save life; After the flood all humankind has returned to clay; the plain is flat as a roof; Instead of the flood, a lion, a wolf, famine or plague should have diminished the people; The mother goddess bars the god who caused the flood from the offering, for he acted without counsel; Huge measured quantities of bitumen, pitch and oil are poured into the kiln and the hull; The hero slaughters oxen and sheep and gives the workers beer, oil and wine like river water, so they feast as at the New Year festival; What sets the flood in motion: God's decision on violence, or the rejected prophet's prayer; The chief god sees the boat and is enraged that a living being escaped: 'no man should survive!'; What the ark contains; Besides kin and animals, craftsmen of every skill are taken aboard; The god gives the hero a cover story: Enlil hates me, I am going down to the Apsû, and he will rain abundance on you (bread-cakes in the morning, a torrent of wheat in the evening) - an ambiguous promise of the coming flood; How the ark is described; and 61 more.

Only in The Flood (full read): Clean animals taken aboard by sevens, unclean by pairs; Flood events given exact calendar dates (year of hero's life, month, day); Rain or flood lasts forty days and forty nights; A dove returns with an olive leaf in its beak; Seven days pass between the warning or boarding and the onset of the flood; Angels object that the new human will corrupt the earth and shed blood while they praise God; When the water overflowed God carried 'you' in the running ship (al-jariya) as a reminder for retaining ears [divergence between the texts]; What sets the flood in motion: God's decision on violence, or the rejected prophet's prayer [divergence between the texts]; How the ark is described [divergence between the texts]; What the flood hero does when the vessel comes to rest [divergence between the texts]; What God says of later generations after the flood: no repeat, or punishment to come [contrast between the texts]; How the flood waters are stopped and subside [divergence between the texts]; and 26 more.

matches.label: A god gives a human knowledge of 'heaven and earth' and a higher divine voice remarks on it
matches.note: A higher divine voice questions the human's privilege: Anu 'why did Ea disclose to a worthless (lā banīta) human what belongs to heaven and earth?'; the angels 'will you place on it one who will corrupt it and shed blood?' Then the knowledge is shown: Adam is taught the names and God says 'I know the unseen of the heavens and the earth (ghayb al-samāwāt wa-l-arḍ)'. In Adapa the objector is the high god and the human was taught by a lesser one; in 2:30-33 the objectors are the angels and the teacher is God.

Adam and his wife eat (fa-akalā minhā) from what Satan called shajarat al-khuld, against God's command. The life-food is refused out of obedience to the adviser; the 'immortality' tree is eaten out of obedience to the adviser.

Only in Ziusudra (Eridu Genesis, ETCSL 1.7.4, segments C-E): The flood storm rages for seven days and seven nights; A goddess laments the destruction of the people decreed by the gods; The sun god appears after the flood and shines into the boat through an opening the hero makes; Animals taken aboard (no pairing specified); The gods grant the flood hero life like a god, eternal life; The flood hero is settled in a far land (Dilmun) where the sun rises; The gods are made to swear an oath binding them to the decision to destroy humankind; The verdict of the divine assembly to destroy is declared irrevocable; Seventh ancestor walks with God and is taken without dying; Hero blessed on leaving the vessel; Hero singled out as righteous or pious; Hero offers sacrifice after leaving the vessel; and 4 more.

Only in BD 125 (pNu): the second declaration of innocence, addressed to the 42 judges: Denial: the speaker did no wrong although he saw evil; Denial: the speaker has not diminished (encroached on) fields or interfered with the field survey; Denial with exception: the speaker has not quarrelled, except over his own property; Denial / prohibition of eavesdropping or spying on others; A list of renounced sins in fixed form: not stealing, not killing, not lying / slandering, not committing adultery; Denial: the speaker has not driven off the cattle of the god's estate nor blocked a god in his procession; The divine judges of the dead live on the evildoers and drink their blood on the day of reckoning; Denial: the speaker has not shortened the grain measure or the land measure nor tampered with the weights or plummet of the balance; The dead person recites before the divine judges a long series of denials, 'I have not done X', to prove his innocence.

Only in BD 125 (pMaiherperi): the 42 addresses: Denial: the speaker has not made anyone go hungry, made anyone weep, or caused anyone pain; A series of 'I/they shall not' clauses covering theft, adultery, killing and lying, spoken before an authority [divergence between the texts].

Only in Al-Hujurat: lowering voices, verifying reports, reconciling believers, backbiting and the peoples and tribes: Those who call the prophet from outside his private chambers (hujurat) lack understanding; they should wait until he comes out; They count their submission a favor to the prophet; rather God has done them a favor in guiding them; Let no people mock another, nor women other women, nor defame one another or insult with nicknames; If two groups of believers fight, make peace between them; fight the one that transgresses until it returns to God's command; The bedouin say 'we believe'; rather say 'we have submitted (aslamna)', for faith has not yet entered your hearts; The believers are nothing but brothers, so make peace between your brothers; One origin (one father, one pair, one God) as ground for conduct toward others [divergence between the texts]; Believers must not put themselves before God and his messenger, nor raise their voices above the prophet's or shout to him; Humanity created from a male and a female and made into peoples (shu'ub) and tribes to know one another; the noblest is the most pious; 'Have we not all one father? Has not one God created us? matches.label: A list of renounced sins in fixed form: not stealing, not killing, not lying / slandering, not committing adultery
matches.note: Before the 42 judges: 'I have not stolen ... I have killed no man ... I have told no lie ... I have not slept with a married woman'; the women's pledge: 'not to associate anything with God, not to steal, not to commit zinā, not to kill their children, not to bring slander'. A fixed list of negations covering theft, killing, falsehood and sexual sin; a retrospective declaration of innocence vs. a pledge for the future.

matches.note: Keepers of the gate of the hereafter stop and question the arriving dead, then admit him. The test changes: secret names and a claim of purity, against whether the messengers were heeded; 'pure' is claimed by the dead in BD and pronounced by the keepers in Q.

Shared motifs, rarest first: A series of 'I/they shall not' clauses covering theft, adultery, killing and lying, spoken before an authority [divergence between the texts] (weight 7.1); Prohibitions of murder, adultery, theft and false witness (weight 5.7). Pair score 12.7.

Only in BD 125 (pYuya): the 42 addresses: Denial with exception: the speaker has not quarrelled, except over his own property; Denial: the speaker has not practised grain usury (ḥnw.yt); Denial: the speaker has not been greedy, puffed up or self-exalting, and his wants were not excessive beyond his own property; Each denial of the confession is addressed to a different named judge ('O Wide-strider who came from Heliopolis, I have done no wrong'); Denials of faults of speech: not lying, not chattering, not hot or loud speech, not eavesdropping, not slandering, not deaf to words of truth; Denial: the speaker has not reviled a god, the king or the god of his town; Denial: the speaker has not had sexual relations with a male (nk nkk, 'copulate with a catamite'); Sexual relations with a neighbor's wife are forbidden.

Only in Al-Mumtahana: no affection for God's enemies, Abraham's excellent example, examining emigrant women, and the women's pledge: Abraham and those with him are an excellent example: they declared themselves quit of their people and their gods, with enmity until they believe; Except Abraham's saying to his father 'I will ask forgiveness for you, though I have no power for you before God'; They despair of the hereafter as the unbelievers despair of those in the graves; Believers must not take God's enemies, who expelled the prophet, as allies (awliya') or secretly show them affection; Prohibition of killing one's children; Do not hold on to marriage ties with unbelieving women; dowries are reckoned between the communities; Believing women who emigrate are to be examined; if believers, they are not returned to the unbelievers, whose dowries are repaid; The women's pledge (bay'at al-nisa'): not to associate anything with God, steal, commit adultery, kill their children, bring a fabricated slander, or disobey in what is right; Abraham declares to his father and people that he is free of what they worship, except the one who created him; Dissolving marriages with women outside the community [divergence between the texts]; God does not forbid kindness and justice toward those who did not fight you over religion or expel you; Neither your blood-ties nor your children will benefit you on the Day of Resurrection; and 9 more.

Only in BD 125 (pTurin 1791, Ptolemaic): title and first declaration of innocence: Denial: the speaker has not ordered anyone to be killed (beside not killing himself); No one is to be burdened with more than he is able to do [divergence between the texts]; The dead person announces to the judge: I have come to you, I have brought you Maat (truth/justice) and driven out wrong; Denial: the speaker has not held back the (irrigation) water in its season nor built a dam against flowing water; Denial: the speaker has not imposed on workers more work in a day than could be done; Denial: the speaker has not taken milk from the mouth of a suckling child; Forty-two divine judges sit with the god of the dead in the hall of judgment, each addressed by an epithet and a place of origin; The dead declares 'I am pure' four times, his purity being that of the great phoenix (benu) of Herakleopolis; Denial: the speaker has not shortened the grain measure or the land measure nor tampered with the weights or plummet of the balance; Denial: the speaker has not had sexual relations with a male (nk nkk, 'copulate with a catamite'); The dead person comes to the Hall of the Two Truths (Maat) to be judged before the great god and separated from the sins he has committed; The dead person claims to know the names of the god and his judges, and this knowledge protects him from their harm; and 1 more.

Only in Al-Rahman: the Merciful taught the Quran; sun and moon by reckoning; clay and smokeless fire; the two seas and the barrier: God raised the sky and set the Balance: do not transgress in the balance; weigh with justice and do not skimp; Lord of the two easts and the two wests (the solstitial sunrises and sunsets); The Merciful (al-Rahman) taught the Quran, created man and taught him clear speech (bayan); From the two seas come pearls and coral (marjan); The divine balance does not tilt, therefore a human judge may not tilt it [divergence between the texts]; A creation litany with a refrain after every line [divergence between the texts]; The text addresses jinn and humans together in the dual ('you two', al-thaqalan, 'the two weighty ones'); All in heaven and earth ask of him; every day he is engaged in some affair (kull yawm huwa fi sha'n); The deity made or presides over the balance; do not tamper with it or make it short; A god sets up or holds the scales so that weighing in trade is just; Earth and heavens will perish and wear out like a garment, changed like clothing, but God remains the same; Man created from ringing clay like pottery, the jinn from a smokeless flame of fire (marij min nar); and 14 more.

evidence.text: Read side by side in both originals (alignments/ane-quran/23-ane-quran.yaml).
Shared motifs, rarest first: At the judgment the dead state whether they fed the hungry [divergence between the texts] (weight 7.3). Pair score 7.3.

Only in BD 125 (pTurin 1791): address to the gods, works of mercy, gate and Thoth, late version: Self-praise of the just: I gave bread to the hungry, water to the thirsty, clothes to the naked (and a ferry to the boatless); The judge's messengers inflict slaughter and punishment, and there is no mercy in their faces; The dead has purified himself in a sacred lake (the southern pool, the field of locusts) where the gods' crew washes; Each part of the gate (jambs, lintel, bolt, doorkeeper, floor, even the soles of the feet) refuses passage until the dead says its secret name; The just one's front, back and middle are pure; no limb of his is without Maat; Gate-guardians interrogate the dead: who are you, what is your name, where did you pass, what did you see, what did they give you?; The just one lives on Maat and feeds on Maat; the divine judges too are said to live on Maat, with no lie in their bodies; The dwelling of Osiris has a roof of fire, walls of living uraeus serpents and a floor of flood water; In the judgment of the dead the heart is weighed on a balance against Maat; Anubis checks the plummet and Thoth records the result; The dead declares himself without wrong, without sin and without any witness against him; there is no one he has harmed; Thoth, the 'interpreter of the Two Lands', receives the purified dead and announces him to Osiris; The justified dead is told: your bread is the Udjat eye, your beer is the Udjat eye, your offering on earth is the Udjat eye; and 3 more.

Only in The cloaked one: the call, the opponent, and the nineteen: The people of paradise ask the damned what brought them to hell; they answer: we did not pray, feed the poor, and we denied the day; Those who turn from the reminder are like startled wild asses fleeing from a lion (qaswara); Every soul is held in pledge (rahina) for what it has earned; Each of the deniers wants to be given scrolls unrolled (personally revealed) to him; Over hell are nineteen; its keepers are angels whose number is made a test; God created a man alone, gave him extended wealth and sons present at his side; yet he wants more and stubbornly opposes the signs; The companions of the right (ashab al-yamin, al-maymana) are saved; the companions of the left (al-mash'ama) are damned; The intercession of intercessors will not benefit the damned; no soul has power to help another; How many wardens or demons are set over the underworld or hell [shared matter] [divergence between the texts]; The people wash their garments to prepare for God's appearance; You will not will unless God wills; Prophet wraps his face in his mantle on hearing God; and 8 more.

Only in Report even father and mother; if a city, a house or one man sins (CTH 133 §§5-12): If a city within the land sins it is killed with its men; if a house within a city sins that house dies with its people; if one man sins, he alone; The vassal people's troop levy is fixed (from 150 to 60 heavy-armed men) and must be of free men, not servants or hirelings; Whether an offender's household and kin share his punishment [contrast between the texts]; Any letter or messenger arriving from the enemy or a foreign land must be seized and sent on to the king; The oath binds not only those present but their sons and grandsons and all who will exist in days to come; Fugitives who flee from one realm to the other must be handed back; The sworn party must report any seditious or evil word heard against the king, whether from a brother, the king's own seed, an official, a friend or anyone, and must not conceal it.

matches.label: Whether one who crosses over from the other party is examined and returned [neutral]
matches.note: Treaty clause: if a servant of Paddatiššu plots against his lord and enters Hatti, and Paddatiššu writes 'he rebelled against me, give him back', then 'if the word is true they shall return the fugitive'; if he denies it, notables of Kizzuwatna swear by the gods and he is returned (§2:15-28). Q 60:10, on those who come over from the other side: 'examine them (fa-mtaḥinūhunna) ... if you know them to be believers do not return them to the unbelievers ... and give (the husbands) what they spent'. Both set a test for the one who crosses over between two parties; the test leads to return in the treaty, to refusal of return, with repayment, in the Quran.

matches.label: Moving a sacred festival or month out of its fixed time is forbidden
matches.note: Both forbid moving sacred time. matches.note: In the husband's house the wife asks the young man to sleep with her: 'eḫu-wa-mu-za katta šēš' (come, sleep with me), and he says no (UL memmaḫḫun). In the Hittite she sends her daughters with the message (§2:16); in the Quran she locks the doors herself (ghallaqati l-abwāb).

Only in The great river bound everything; Kamrušepa conjures and looses it; the child bound and loosed limb by limb (CTH 390 §36-46): The patient was 'bound' in each body part, hair, skull, nose, ears, mouth, tongue, throat, chest, lungs, liver, genitals, bladder, anus, knees, hands; each is conjured and loosed; The goddess drives to the river and conjures it, and the river, mountains, valleys, animals and throne are loosed (lā- 'to loosen') item by item; A great river binds its flood, the fish, the high mountains, deep valleys, the storm god's meadow, the eagle's wings, eels, the stag under the oak, panther, wolf, lion, wild goat and its milk, and the throne of the protective god; A word passes from one deity to the next down a chain (Ištar to Maliya, Maliya to Pirwa, Pirwa to Kamrušepa) until the healing goddess acts; A message goes to the goddess (Kamrušepa, the mother goddess), who answers 'bring the Old Woman' to cleanse or conjure the patient; The god is one who knows how to bind and to release; The ritualist says: are these my words? They are the words of the Sun god and of Kamrušepa; The gods, at a loss before the angry god, ask one another 'how shall we act, what shall we do?'.

evidence.text: Shared motifs, rarest first: The afflicting deity is told: take this one (the carrier animal) for yourself, and we give you another (a goat, a pure mouse) to eat (weight 7.3); Formula: take the evil out of him and give it to the evil men, the enemies; to the patients give life, vigour and long years (weight 7.1); Analogy of the launderers: as they clean the linen and pluck off the lint until it is white, so may the gods clean the evil illness out of this man's body (weight 7.1); White wool or a bowstring is drawn over the patient from the feet up to the head and down the back, then taken off and laid in a basket, pulling the evil out of every limb (weight 7.1); Tin wrapped in a bowstring is tied on the patient's right hand and foot, then wound on a mouse, which is released to carry the evil over high mountains, deep valleys and far roads (weight 7.1); Wood and grain are roasted and the fire quenched with water: as I have quenched this, so may the evil be quenched over the patients (weight 7.1); The afflicting deity is told to stop fighting the patients and fight this bolt (a model door-bolt) instead, and drive the evil away with it (weight 7.1); Living goat bears the people's sins away into the wilderness (weight 6.2). Pair score 55.9.

Only in Ambazzi's ritual for Alauwaima, the mouse released, a goat in its place, metals for good speech before the gods (CTH 391.1 §13-28): The deity is asked to give the patient life, health, vigour, long years and the sight of the eyes; A little of every metal and stone (silver, gold, lapis, carnelian, iron, tin, copper, bronze) is strewn for the deity, who is asked to speak good for the patient before all the gods; Choice portions of the victim (right ear, liver, heart, right shoulder, breast, hoof) are roasted and set before the gods on bread and leaves; the rest is cooked and eaten by the participants.

evidence.text: Shared motifs, rarest first: The afflicting deity is told: take this one (the carrier animal) for yourself, and we give you another (a goat, a pure mouse) to eat (weight 7.3); Formula: take the evil out of him and give it to the evil men, the enemies; to the patients give life, vigour and long years (weight 7.1); Analogy of the launderers: as they clean the linen and pluck off the lint until it is white, so may the gods clean the evil illness out of this man's body (weight 7.1); White wool or a bowstring is drawn over the patient from the feet up to the head and down the back, then taken off and laid in a basket, pulling the evil out of every limb (weight 7.1); Tin wrapped in a bowstring is tied on the patient's right hand and foot, then wound on a mouse, which is released to carry the evil over high mountains, deep valleys and far roads (weight 7.1); Wood and grain are roasted and the fire quenched with water: as I have quenched this, so may the evil be quenched over the patients (weight 7.1); The afflicting deity is told to stop fighting the patients and fight this bolt (a model door-bolt) instead, and drive the evil away with it (weight 7.1); Living goat bears the people's sins away into the wilderness (weight 6.2). Pair score 55.9.

Only in Ambazzi's ritual for Tarpatassa 'who stands in front', the second pure mouse (CTH 391.1 §29-43): A little of every metal and stone (silver, gold, lapis, carnelian, iron, tin, copper, bronze) is strewn for the deity, who is asked to speak good for the patient before all the gods; Choice portions of the victim (right ear, liver, heart, right shoulder, breast, hoof) are roasted and set before the gods on bread and leaves; the rest is cooked and eaten by the participants.
Ambazzi's ritual for Zarniza and Tarpatassa, quenching, wool, the launderers, the mouse (CTH 391.1 §1-12): tagged by Claude (model), reading the Hittite.
Ambazzi's ritual for Tarpatassa 'who stands in front', the second pure mouse (CTH 391.1 §29-43): tagged by Claude (model), reading the Hittite.

Only in Alli of Arzawa against sorcery, the clay figurines with tongues and the sorcery handed back (CTH 402 §1-8): May the sorcery be the sorceress's headdress, her belt and her shoes: may she put them on and take back what she did; The 'Sun god of the hand' (kiššeraš UTU) is called to see the sorcerers and to recognise whether a man or a woman did the bewitching; The evil, carried in ritual materials, is given to horses as fodder and to dogs as a morsel; Dialogue in the rite: the mortal says 'we are tired, we dare no more, take it back' and the figurines answer 'bring it, we will carry it off'; A hunter figure with bow, arrows and four dogs is to put on, take up and carry away the sorcery, raking and shovelling it up; The bewitched person is seated facing the Sun god while the practitioner works; Clay figurines of the sorcerers, male and female, are made with tongues inside them, a clay basket full of tongues and a clay donkey to carry it; Stones or rites serve to turn back a curse onto its sender; The practitioner takes the sorcery off the patient and throws or gives it back to the sorcerer or its 'owner', who is to carry it; A ritual opens 'Thus (says) N., the Old Woman / augur / man of town X', naming the practitioner who speaks the rite in the first person.

Only in The heirs of the Book, the Gardens of Eden and the cries of the damned: God made humans successors (khala'if) on the earth; Heirs of the Book are of three kinds: one who wrongs himself, one who is moderate, and one foremost in good deeds; The guilty, heads bowed before their Lord, beg to be returned to do good; God holds the heavens and the earth lest they cease; if they ceased, no one else could hold them; If God took people to task for what they earned he would not leave a creature on the earth's back, but he defers them to a set term; Paradise is the abode of permanence where no toil or weariness touches the blessed and grief is removed; The evil plot or sorcery turns back upon its own author; The evil plot encompasses only its own authors; In paradise the righteous are adorned with gold bracelets and pearls and wear silk; The god (alone) holds the heavens (and earth) in place: the bond or rope of heaven, holding back the sky; In hell the damned neither die nor live; The way (sunna) of God with those who passed before: you will find no change in God's way; and 3 more.

Shared motifs, rarest first: Sorcery is done by binding or knotting (weight 7.7). Pair score 7.7.

Only in Alli ritual, coloured threads take off the colours of sorcery, white wool purifies (CTH 402 §9-19): Threads of black, red, yellow-green, blue and white wool take off the patient the blackness, redness, yellowness, 'blue day' and binding of sorcery and are wound round the figurines; The drunkenness caused by sorcery is taken off the patient and the sorcerer made drunk through the figurines; Whether someone harmed the patient before the gods or before mortals, the harm is to be removed; Analogic spell: as white wool appeases fierce hostility, so may it purify the sorcery and impurity and make the person pure before all; Whoever 'bound' the patient by sorcery, the practitioner takes it from all his limbs; The practitioner takes the sorcery off the patient and throws or gives it back to the sorcerer or its 'owner', who is to carry it; Analogic spell: as this substance (seed, water, soap, clay, wool, dough) is treated or acts, so may the evil, impurity or sorcery be treated.

Only in Sincerity, daybreak and mankind: God's unity and the two refuges: Refuge from the evil of darkness (or the moon) when it settles (ghasiq idha waqab); Refuge from the evil of an envier when he envies (evil eye); God is al-Samad (the Eternal Refuge, the solid one who needs nothing); Triple title: Lord of mankind, King of mankind, God of mankind; Refuge from the evil of the slinking whisperer (al-waswas al-khannas) who whispers in people's breasts, from jinn and humans; Calling on a divine name or seeking refuge with God protects a person in the dark of night; God does not beget and was not begotten [contrast between the texts]; A deity is called king of (all) mankind; Protection against beings or evil of the night, invoked with the coming of dawn; Protective formula 'Say: I seek refuge with the Lord of...' (qul a'udhu bi-rabbi) against named evils; Witchcraft worked by a (female) witch through knots or bonds, from which release or refuge is sought; Psalm used as protection against demons and harm (later amulet and 'song of plagues'); and 10 more.

matches.note: Mallidunna's rite for the Sun: 'the Sun deity goes (dUTU-uš=kan paizzi); [they] light nine torches (9 GIŠzupparu lukkanzi)', 'as soon as the Sun deity [goes] down (katta)'. 6:78: Abraham sees the sun rising, 'this is my lord, this is greater', 'fa-lammā afalat', and when it set he said 'my people, I am free of what you associate'. Only in Mallidunna's ritual for the Sun god, the three pairs of eyes of the Sun (CTH 403.1): The deity is said to drink her fill (niku-) at the offering; The gods are given offerings one after another in turn (irḫa-); The Sun god has three pairs of eyes: of watching, of appeasement and of governing and judgment; Torches are lit as the Sun deity goes down; A ritual opens 'Thus (says) N., the Old Woman / augur / man of town X', naming the practitioner who speaks the rite in the first person; The sun god is judge who searches out verdicts, placed over heaven and earth; The ritualist sets food and drink before the angry god and invokes him (mugai-): eat, drink, still your hunger and thirst, come back and be at peace.

Only in Abraham, Azar and the star, moon and sun: Abraham's people dispute with him; he fears none of their gods; God showed Abraham the kingdom (malakūt) of the heavens and the earth; Abraham's father is named Āzar; Abraham: 'I do not love things that set' (lā uḥibbu l-āfilīn); Which of the two parties has more right to security? Those who believe without mixing in wrong; God takes the patriarch outside and tells him to count the stars; God takes the patriarch outside and tells him to count the stars [divergence between the texts]; A star, the moon or the sun is identified as the (high) god [divergence between the texts]; If he is a god, let him defend himself [divergence between the texts]; Prohibition of worshipping sun, moon, stars, the host of heaven [divergence between the texts]; Patriarch believes God and it is counted to him as righteousness; Follow the religion (milla) of Abraham the ḥanīf, who was no idolater; and 4 more.

Shared motifs, rarest first: Simile: to recognise someone as father and mother recognise their sons (weight 7.7). Pair score 7.7.

Only in Offerings to the Sun god, 'as the ewe recognises her lamb' (CTH 403.3.1): The god's image is turned with its eyes toward the king, queen and princes; The Sun god is let into the house through the window; Analogic prayer: as the ewe recognises her lamb, the cow her calf and father and mother their sons, so may the god recognise (keep favour with) the king, queen and princes; At the end of the rite the 'lord of the deity' or the officiant takes what lies before the deity and returns it to the temple; The participants 'drink' a deity a set number of times, standing or sitting, as a ritual act of communion; On the god's return the mother recognises her son again, the ewe her lamb and the cow her calf; The ritualist sets food and drink before the angry god and invokes him (mugai-): eat, drink, still your hunger and thirst, come back and be at peace.

Only in The change of qibla: The direction of prayer (qibla) is changed toward the Sacred Mosque; fools ask why; Believers made a middle community (umma wasat), witnesses over mankind, with the messenger a witness over them; God sees the prophet turning his face toward heaven and grants him a qibla he is pleased with; To each a direction he faces: so race toward good deeds; Abraham and Ishmael pray that a messenger be raised from among their offspring; The People of the Book recognize the truth as they recognize their own sons; The direction faced in prayer [divergence between the texts]; Prayers made toward the temple (or toward the land, city and house when in exile) are heard in heaven; Leader prays 'remember me, my God, for good' for his deeds; Who bears witness to God's oneness [divergence between the texts].

evidence.text: Shared motifs, rarest first: A pot waved over the patients is called the substitute for their heads and broken; they smash another vessel with their feet, breaking all the evil words and curses (weight 7.7); The patients' bodies are wiped with a 'plant of the Sun' named tiwariya, wiping off the evil words of mouth and tongue (weight 7.3); Seven standing stones (huwaši) are set between two fires and kicked over: as these stones fall, so may the words of mouth and tongue that came on the patients fall (weight 7.3); Water is poured into an ox horn and sealed by the patients: only when the ancient kings return and examine the land and its customs may the seal be broken (weight 7.3); The patients pour water with natron over their heads and wash their hands and eyes (weight 7.3); After passing through the fire the patients throw off their fine garments and the Old Woman takes them (weight 7.3); Fires are lit to right and left and the patients pass through the middle of the fire (weight 7.3); A text ends with a note on its source or on where it was written (weight 4.2). Pair score 56.0.

Only in Maštigga ritual, second manuscript group, salamander to the sealed horn and colophon of Ḫanikkuili (CTH 404.1.II §20-44): A clay vessel of Šaušga with oil, wool and barley is held under the patients' garment: may it release them to wellbeing and life and hide the evil away in an evil thing; A sheep is declared the patients' nakkušši (carrier of evil) with mouth and tongue, presented to the Sun, but not killed: the Old Woman takes it for herself; A salamander wrapped in blue and red wool is waved over the patients: may its swift foot carry off the evil tongue on its back and with its teeth; Seven copper (or bronze) nails are driven into the ground: may the evil be nailed down with its mouth and tongue, with the Sun's help; Seven vessels filled with wine, oil, honey, fruit, sinew, salt and fat are emptied one by one into the hearth and broken: may it break with mouth and tongue; The exalted Sun god is declared to stand behind (guarantee the treatment of) mouth and tongue; The substitute animal is slaughtered down into a dug pit, laid in it with sweet bread and wine, and covered with earth; An animal (sheep, black sheep, puppy) is held over the patients and declared their substitute (tarpalli-) for their heads and whole persons.

Shared motifs, rarest first: A substitute (animal or person) is given to the deity in place of a human life [divergence between the texts] (weight 7.1). Pair score 7.1.

Only in Maštigga ritual, sheep and black sheep as substitutes, the patients spit into their mouths, the piglet buried (CTH 404.1.I §20-25): The black substitute sheep, after the patients have spat into its mouth, is slaughtered, dismembered and burned whole on a hearth with honey and olive oil poured over it; A piglet fattened on grass and grain is waved, killed and buried: as it will not see the sky or the other piglets again, so may the evil curses not see the patients again; The ritual remains carrying the evil are buried in a pit, covered, levelled and pinned down with pegs, and the dark earth is to hold them so that they never come up again; The patients spit into the mouth of the substitute animal: 'you have spat out the evil curses'; Ritual materials (seeds, breads, cords, an animal) are waved (wahnu-) over the patient and through the house to absorb the evil; The substitute animal is slaughtered down into a dug pit, laid in it with sweet bread and wine, and covered with earth; An animal (sheep, black sheep, puppy) is held over the patients and declared their substitute (tarpalli-) for their heads and whole persons.

Only in Abraham's dream and the near-sacrifice of his son: God ransomed the son with a great sacrifice (dhibh 'azim); When both had submitted he laid him on his forehead (talla-hu li-l-jabin); The father sees in a dream that he is sacrificing his son; The son of the sacrifice is not named; Isaac's birth is announced only after the episode (read as Ishmael by many exegetes); An angel calls from heaven to stop the sacrifice at the last moment; Father binds his son on the altar and lifts the knife; God commands a father to sacrifice his son; God commands a father to sacrifice his son [divergence between the texts]; The father lays the son down for the sacrifice [divergence between the texts]; Who the son to be sacrificed is and how he is named [divergence between the texts]; Lot believes in Abraham, who declares 'I am emigrating to my Lord'; A ram caught in a thicket is sacrificed in place of the son; and 11 more.

evidence.text: Shared motifs, rarest first: A clay vessel of Šaušga with oil, wool and barley is held under the patients' garment: may it release them to wellbeing and life and hide the evil away in an evil thing (weight 7.3); Seven copper (or bronze) nails are driven into the ground: may the evil be nailed down with its mouth and tongue, with the Sun's help (weight 7.3); A sheep is declared the patients' nakkušši (carrier of evil) with mouth and tongue, presented to the Sun, but not killed: the Old Woman takes it for herself (weight 7.3); A salamander wrapped in blue and red wool is waved over the patients: may its swift foot carry off the evil tongue on its back and with its teeth (weight 7.3); Seven vessels filled with wine, oil, honey, fruit, sinew, salt and fat are emptied one by one into the hearth and broken: may it break with mouth and tongue (weight 7.3); The exalted Sun god is declared to stand behind (guarantee the treatment of) mouth and tongue (weight 7.3); The substitute animal is slaughtered down into a dug pit, laid in it with sweet bread and wine, and covered with earth (weight 7.1); An animal (sheep, black sheep, puppy) is held over the patients and declared their substitute (tarpalli-) for their heads and whole persons (weight 6.6). Pair score 57.7.

Only in Maštigga ritual, clay and cumin, the salamander and puppy, Šaušga's vessel, the carrier sheep and the seven nails (CTH 404.1.I §26-38): The patients place their hand on the bread, cheese and wine before the Old Woman breaks and offers it; Analogic spell: as this clay will not return to the riverbank, black cumin will not turn white nor become another seed, and this dough will not go into the gods' bread, so may the evil tongue not go into the patients' bodies; The patients spit into the mouth of the substitute animal: 'you have spat out the evil curses'; The Old Woman sprinkles the patients with water and waves dough over them: 'be pure again of mouth and tongue'; Living goat bears the people's sins away into the wilderness.

Only in Maštigga ritual, second manuscript group, salamander to the sealed horn and colophon of Ḫanikkuili (CTH 404.1.II §20-44): A pot waved over the patients is called the substitute for their heads and broken; they smash another vessel with their feet, breaking all the evil words and curses; Seven standing stones (huwaši) are set between two fires and kicked over: as these stones fall, so may the words of mouth and tongue that came on the patients fall; The patients' bodies are wiped with a 'plant of the Sun' named tiwariya, wiping off the evil words of mouth and tongue; After passing through the fire the patients throw off their fine garments and the Old Woman takes them; Fires are lit to right and left and the patients pass through the middle of the fire; The patients pour water with natron over their heads and wash their hands and eyes; Water is poured into an ox horn and sealed by the patients: only when the ancient kings return and examine the land and its customs may the seal be broken; A text ends with a note on its source or on where it was written.

evidence.text: Shared motifs, rarest first: A clay vessel of Šaušga with oil, wool and barley is held under the patients' garment: may it release them to wellbeing and life and hide the evil away in an evil thing (weight 7.3); Seven copper (or bronze) nails are driven into the ground: may the evil be nailed down with its mouth and tongue, with the Sun's help (weight 7.3); Analogic spell: as this clay will not return to the riverbank, black cumin will not turn white nor become another seed, and this dough will not go into the gods' bread, so may the evil tongue not go into the patients' bodies (weight 7.3); A salamander wrapped in blue and red wool is waved over the patients: may its swift foot carry off the evil tongue on its back and with its teeth (weight 7.3); A sheep is declared the patients' nakkušši (carrier of evil) with mouth and tongue, presented to the Sun, but not killed: the Old Woman takes it for herself (weight 7.3); Seven vessels filled with wine, oil, honey, fruit, sinew, salt and fat are emptied one by one into the hearth and broken: may it break with mouth and tongue (weight 7.3); The exalted Sun god is declared to stand behind (guarantee the treatment of) mouth and tongue (weight 7.3); The Old Woman sprinkles the patients with water and waves dough over them: 'be pure again of mouth and tongue' (weight 7.1); The patients spit into the mouth of the substitute animal: 'you have spat out the evil curses' (weight 7.1); An animal (sheep, black sheep, puppy) is held over the patients and declared their substitute (tarpalli-) for their heads and whole persons (weight 6.6). Pair score 72.1.

Only in Maštigga ritual, clay and cumin, the salamander and puppy, Šaušga's vessel, the carrier sheep and the seven nails (CTH 404.1.I §26-38): The patients place their hand on the bread, cheese and wine before the Old Woman breaks and offers it; The substitute animal is slaughtered down into a dug pit, laid in it with sweet bread and wine, and covered with earth; Living goat bears the people's sins away into the wilderness.

Only in Maštigga ritual, third manuscript group for a single patient, the tongues nailed on Mount Amanakkipalu (CTH 404.1.III): Seven tongues of clay are fixed into the ground and the practitioner declares that father Sun has nailed down the tongues of the day of quarrel (on Mount Amanakkipalu); Seven standing stones (huwaši) are set between two fires and kicked over: as these stones fall, so may the words of mouth and tongue that came on the patients fall; The patients' bodies are wiped with a 'plant of the Sun' named tiwariya, wiping off the evil words of mouth and tongue; After passing through the fire the patients throw off their fine garments and the Old Woman takes them; Fires are lit to right and left and the patients pass through the middle of the fire; White and black wool wrapped in fat, called tiššatwa, is held over the patients to take away what they said with mouth and tongue; The patients pour water with natron over their heads and wash their hands and eyes; Water is poured into an ox horn and sealed by the patients: only when the ancient kings return and examine the land and its customs may the seal be broken; A text ends with a note on its source or on where it was written.
Maštigga ritual, clay and cumin, the salamander and puppy, Šaušga's vessel, the carrier sheep and the seven nails (CTH 404.1.I §26-38): tagged by Claude (model), reading the Hittite.
Maštigga ritual, third manuscript group for a single patient, the tongues nailed on Mount Amanakkipalu (CTH 404.1.III): tagged by Claude (model), reading the Hittite.

Seven copper (or bronze) nails are driven into the ground: may the evil be nailed down with its mouth and tongue, with the Sun's help (weight 7.3); Seven standing stones (huwaši) are set between two fires and kicked over: as these stones fall, so may the words of mouth and tongue that came on the patients fall (weight 7.3); The patients' bodies are wiped with a 'plant of the Sun' named tiwariya, wiping off the evil words of mouth and tongue (weight 7.3); A sheep is declared the patients' nakkušši (carrier of evil) with mouth and tongue, presented to the Sun, but not killed: the Old Woman takes it for herself (weight 7.3); A salamander wrapped in blue and red wool is waved over the patients: may its swift foot carry off the evil tongue on its back and with its teeth (weight 7.3); Water is poured into an ox horn and sealed by the patients: only when the ancient kings return and examine the land and its customs may the seal be broken (weight 7.3); Seven vessels filled with wine, oil, honey, fruit, sinew, salt and fat are emptied one by one into the hearth and broken: may it break with mouth and tongue (weight 7.3); The patients pour water with natron over their heads and wash their hands and eyes (weight 7.3); After passing through the fire the patients throw off their fine garments and the Old Woman takes them (weight 7.3); The exalted Sun god is declared to stand behind (guarantee the treatment of) mouth and tongue (weight 7.3); Fires are lit to right and left and the patients pass through the middle of the fire (weight 7.3); An animal (sheep, black sheep, puppy) is held over the patients and declared their substitute (tarpalli-) for their heads and whole persons (weight 6.6); A text ends with a note on its source or on where it was written (weight 4.2). Pair score 99.0.

Only in Maštigga ritual, second manuscript group, salamander to the sealed horn and colophon of Ḫanikkuili (CTH 404.1.II §20-44): A pot waved over the patients is called the substitute for their heads and broken; they smash another vessel with their feet, breaking all the evil words and curses; The substitute animal is slaughtered down into a dug pit, laid in it with sweet bread and wine, and covered with earth.

Only in Maštigga ritual, third manuscript group for a single patient, the tongues nailed on Mount Amanakkipalu (CTH 404.1.III): Analogic spell: as this clay will not return to the riverbank, black cumin will not turn white nor become another seed, and this dough will not go into the gods' bread, so may the evil tongue not go into the patients' bodies; Seven tongues of clay are fixed into the ground and the practitioner declares that father Sun has nailed down the tongues of the day of quarrel (on Mount Amanakkipalu); White and black wool wrapped in fat, called tiššatwa, is held over the patients to take away what they said with mouth and tongue; The patients spit into the mouth of the substitute animal: 'you have spat out the evil curses'; The Old Woman sprinkles the patients with water and waves dough over them: 'be pure again of mouth and tongue'.

Only in Treaty of Tutḫaliya I with Šunaššura, Akkadian version KBo 28.110 (CTH 41.I.1): the ox and its stall, the tablet, the gods: The vassal is to trust a messenger only if his spoken words agree with the words written on the tablet he brings; A rival is condemned by his own earlier answer ('Just so!') to the very case now turned against him; The tablet of a vassal's former oath to a rival overlord is erased, the rival's word rejected and a new tablet made; The great king releases a land from a former overlord's oath, an act of 'release' (andurāru); When the vassal comes before the great king he may see the king's face and no grandee sits above him; Ox knows its owner and the ass its master's crib, but Israel does not know (animals wiser than God's people); Treaty curse: may the gods destroy the oath-breaker's name and seed from the earth; A parity treaty repeats each obligation with the roles of the two kings exchanged ('and for the other the same'); A long roster of the great gods and the gods of each city and land is named as present at the conclusion of the treaty.

Only in Sefire I face A - the treaty of Bar-Gaʾyah of KTK with Matiʿel of Arpad and the gods as witnesses (KAI 222 A 1-13): The gods El and Elyon are invoked as a pair; The witnessing gods are told 'open your eyes to look on the treaty'; The treaty is 'cut' (gzr), the Aramaic counterpart of cutting a covenant; The treaty is concluded before a long list of named gods, paired, ending with heaven and earth, abyss and springs, day and night; The treaty binds the kings, their sons, grandsons, offspring, nobles and whole lands.

Shared motifs, rarest first: A speaker denies having done the deed himself and ascribes it to a higher agent: 'not I (we) did it, but X did it' (weight 7.3). Pair score 7.3.

Only in Building ritual for a new temple, copper nailed under the pillar and foundation stones of nine materials (CTH 413.1 §1-11): Black iron 'of heaven' (meteoric iron) is said to have been brought from heaven for the foundation; Blessing: may the one who built this temple be eternal before the gods, with grandchildren and great-grandchildren; Copper is laid in a pit at the place of the pillar, nailed round with pegs and struck with an iron hammer: as the copper is protective and eternal, so may the temple be on the dark earth; Analogic blessing: as the four corners of the house are eternal on the earth and do not move, so may the patron's wellbeing not turn away; Analogic blessing: as gold is eternal, pure and strong, good for gods and men, so may this temple be eternal and good for the god; The materials of the temple are said to have been brought from named lands and mountains: gold, silver, lapis, alabaster, quartz, copper; The builders declare to the deity: 'not we built this temple; all the gods built it'; Under each corner, pillar, pedestal, hearth and door of a new temple, small foundation stones or models of silver, gold, lapis, quartz, alabaster, iron, copper, bronze and rock are laid; Iron is said to have been brought or sent down from heaven; A new temple or house is built on untouched (dammeli) ground; Several gods each perform a part of the temple's founding (foundation pegs, bricks, oil, oracles).

Only in Badr - angels, slumber, rain and God's throw: Rain is sent down before battle to purify the fighters, remove Satan's filth and make their feet firm; Some believers dispute the call to battle as if driven to death with their eyes open; God covers the fighters with slumber as a security from him before battle; Angels are told to strike the enemy above the necks and on every finger-tip; God reduces the army so that Israel cannot boast its own hand saved it; Hard pressed by a superior enemy, a leader or army calls on God and God answers; Fleeing the battle line is forbidden except as a maneuver or to join another unit; Ruling on soldiers who fear battle [contrast between the texts]; The threatened people cry to God before the decisive encounter [divergence between the texts]; Priest addresses the army before battle: do not fear, God fights for you; God cuts off the last remnant (root, dabir) of a people who denied; The victory is credited to God, not to the fighters [divergence between the texts]; and 6 more.

matches.label: A bird at a ruler's command goes out to a far place, looks, and comes back to report what it saw there
matches.note: §15:67-71 the throne calls the eagle: 'come, I send you to the sea; spy into the green forest (šu-ú-wa-ya) who is there'; §16:73-74 the eagle answers šu-wa-ya-u-un-wa, 'I watched: Išduštaya and Papaya, the ancient goddesses, kneel there', and asked 'what are they doing?' (§17:76) reports 'she holds a distaff, they hold full spindles'. 27:20-24: Solomon misses the hoopoe; it returns: aḥaṭtu bi-mā lam tuḥiṭ bihi wa-jiʾtuka min sabaʾin bi-nabaʾin yaqīn ... innī wajadtu mraʾatan tamlikuhum ... wa-lahā ʿarshun ʿaẓīm, 'I found a woman ruling them... she has a mighty throne'. A bird in the service of a throne goes far, looks, and reports female figures (goddesses spinning; a queen) to its master, with a throne on each side (the speaking throne; the queen's ʿarsh). In the Hittite the bird is sent, in the Quran it goes unbidden and is missed.

Only in The eagle sees the fate goddesses spinning the king's years; the king renewed (CTH 414.1 §15-33): In a ritual a speaker sends the eagle out to spy and report who is in the green forest; All the gods are gathered on the mountain and rejoice in the king and esteem him; The gods take away the king's old age and give him back youth and fighting strength; Grain is poured out and crushed: may the gods give over to evil and crush whoever plans evil against the king; The gods make the king a figure of tin with a head of iron, eagle's eyes and lion's teeth; Lion's and leopard's paws are braided into one so that the king's soul be intertwined with his heart; Litany 'take from him': illness, fear, headache, the evil words of men, revenge, knee and heart illness are taken from the king; Named mountains are told to stay in their place and not drive away the great one; Ancient netherworld goddesses (Išduštaya and Papaya) kneel with distaff and full spindles and spin the king's years; Skilled weaving women and weavers receive figs and raisins and are told to appease the king, his eyes, and take his ills away; The gods give the king many years, and his years have no shortness or limit; The Sun god and the Storm god have handed over (maniyaḫḫ-) the land and the king's house to the king.

Only in Solomon, the speech of birds, the ants, the hoopoe and the Queen of Sheba: Entering Solomon's palace, the queen takes its floor of smooth glass for a pool and bares her legs; The hoopoe returns with sure news from Sabaʾ, knowledge Solomon lacked; Solomon sends the hoopoe to drop his letter before the queen and wait for their reply; Solomon reviews the birds, finds the hoopoe absent and threatens to punish or slaughter it unless it brings a clear excuse; An ʿifrīt of the jinn offers to bring the queen's throne before Solomon rises from his seat; Solomon's letter begins 'In the name of God, the Merciful, the Compassionate' and demands submission; The queen sends a gift to see what the envoys bring back; Solomon rejects the wealth and threatens invasion; The queen confesses she wronged herself and submits with Solomon to God, Lord of the worlds; Solomon has the queen's throne disguised to test whether she recognizes it; she says 'It is as though it were it'; The queen and her people prostrate to the sun instead of God; Solomon inherits from David (knowledge and kingship); Solomon prays to be inspired to thank God for favor to him and his parents and to be admitted among the righteous; and 42 more.

matches.note: §50:209 'as the vine sends roots downward (katta šurkuš) and shoots upward (šarā ... maḫluš)', so the king and queen; §51:213-216 'as the eya-tree is ever growing and does not shed its leaves, so may they flourish and may their words (uddār) be ever-lasting (uktūri)'. 14:24-25 kalimatan ṭayyibatan ka-shajaratin ṭayyibatin aṣluhā thābitun wa-farʿuhā fī s-samāʾi tuʾtī ukulahā kulla ḥīnin, 'a good word is like a good tree: its root firm, its branch in the sky, it gives its fruit at every season'. The same likeness: roots below and growth above, never failing, applied to words. In the Hittite it is a building blessing on the royal couple; in the Quran a parable of the good word.

Only in Old Hittite rituals for the royal couple II - the eagle waved over them and released to the sky (CTH 416 §20-32): Analogy: as the Sun goddess and the Storm god, heaven and earth, are eternal, so may king, queen and children be eternal; Cups are given to the king, the queen, the throne and the hearth; An eagle is presented to the Sun goddess and Storm god (as the royal couple's substitute) while king and queen hold sickle and millstone; An eagle waved over the royal couple is released to the sky and told to tell the Sun goddess and Storm god that king and queen should be eternal; The ritual expert disclaims the act: 'Not I released it; the king and queen released it'; Two palace attendants clash bronze spears together three times; A clay army set on a bread, with a bronze dagger on it, is waved over or spat on by the royal couple and then buried; Wish that the enemy (the enemy land) carry away the evil removed from the royal couple; The ritual expert goes to the house of the (royal) children only when king and queen tell him; once he used to go, now he no longer does; The participants eat and drink at the end of the rite; The carrier figurines and cups are buried in the earth and nailed down so that the evil may not come back up.

matches.note: Who was Mariya and why did he die? A palace maid walked by and he looked at her; the king's father saw it from the window: 'why did you look at her?', and he died for it: 'for looking from afar a man perished; so beware' (§32:269-278). Q 24:30: 'tell the believing men to lower their gaze and guard their private parts; that is purer for them'. The man's look at a woman as the thing to be controlled; a death sentence against a command to look down.

matches.label: Whether a man may take his wife's sister [neutral]
matches.note: Šuppiluliuma gives Ḫuqqana his sister, whose sisters 'of her clan and seed' are many and now his kin; in Ḫayaša 'a man takes his wife's sister', but 'in Hattusa it is not right'; if his wife's sister visits, 'give her to eat and drink ... but do not desire to take her; for this matter they die' (§29:232-245, §30:246-251). Q 4:23 lists among the women forbidden 'that you join two sisters (bayna l-ukhtayn), except what is past'. The wife's sister as a partner: forbidden as kin, on pain of death, in the treaty; forbidden only together with her sister, with past unions excused, in the Quran.
