Only in CTH 51.I §9-15: stipulations - the treaty, aid, fugitives returned one way only, the Euphrat border, brotherhood of Piyaššili and Šattiwazza: Each party swears not to cross the boundary (a river, a heap) into the other's side; The great king says he will bring a dead (ruined) land back to life and restore it to its place; A dead (ruined) land or town is brought back to life [divergence between the texts]; 'How good and pleasant when brothers dwell together in unity'; A fugitive who comes over is not handed back, because returning him is not right under the divine rule; The overlord fixes and seals the vassal's borders for him and his descendants for ever, listing the frontier towns and mountains one by one; The overlord promises that if anyone presses the vassal, he himself, a prince or a great lord will come with troops and chariots and kill the enemy; The treaty tablet ends: whoever changes this treaty, may the named gods (storm god, sun god, city goddesses) be the lords of his oath (avenge it); Fugitives who flee from one realm to the other must be handed back; The sworn party must report any seditious or evil word heard against the king, whether from a brother, the king's own seed, an official, a friend or anyone, and must not conceal it.

Only in Admission to the assembly; camp purity; slaves, interest, vows: Edomites (brothers) and Egyptians (hosts) admitted in the third generation; Harlot's hire and the price of a dog may not be brought to the temple for a vow; Latrine outside the war camp; dig with a spade and cover excrement because God walks in the camp; Man unclean from a nocturnal emission stays outside the camp until evening and washes; Ammonites and Moabites never admitted, for withholding bread and water and hiring Balaam; Whether obligations differ toward insiders and outsiders [contrast between the texts]; You may eat your fill in a neighbor's vineyard or pluck ears by hand, but not carry away or use a sickle; Man with crushed testicles or severed member excluded from the assembly; Mamzer excluded from the assembly to the tenth generation; Protection for someone who seeks refuge [divergence between the texts]; God turned Balaam's curse into a blessing; Whether obligations differ toward insiders and outsiders [response between the texts]; and 4 more.

Only in Captives, instigators, Nuḫašše folk in Hatti, refugees and requests (CTH 53 §§10-14): A people or fugitive passing through the vassal's land must be set safely on the road to the overlord's land with good words, not turned toward the mountains or to another land; Whatever the vassal desires (people, captives, booty) he must ask of the great king; what the king gives he may take, what he does not give he may not take; The vassal may not excuse inaction by saying 'I am bound by oath and treaty; whether the enemy kills them or they kill him, I do not know'; Those who incite rebellion must be seized, put in fetters and delivered to the king, or killed; Fugitives who flee from one realm to the other must be handed back.

Only in Al-Hashr: the first gathering and exile of the Banu Nadir, the cut palms, and the law of fay': The expelled demolish their houses with their own hands and the hands of the believers; Had God not decreed exile (jala') for them, he would have punished them in this world; God expelled the unbelieving People of the Book (the Banu Nadir) from their homes at 'the first gathering' (li-awwal al-hashr); Whatever palm trees (lina) you cut down or left standing on their roots was by God's leave; Later believers pray: forgive us and our brethren who preceded us in faith, and put no rancor in our hearts; Vines or palms of a hostile neighbour are cut down [divergence between the texts]; Whether the enemy's trees may be cut down in a siege [contrast between the texts]; How spoil taken from the enemy is distributed [divergence between the texts]; Fay' (booty gained without cavalry or camels) goes to God, the messenger, kin, orphans, the poor and the wayfarer, so wealth does not circulate only among the rich; They thought their fortresses would protect them from God, but God came from where they did not expect and cast terror into their hearts; The wealth of a ruined or expelled people passes to others who did not have it [divergence between the texts]; The poor emigrants and the hosts who prefer others over themselves even in need; whoever is saved from his own greed succeeds; and 8 more.

Only in Tribute, audience, friend and enemy, wholehearted war (CTH 53 §§5-7): The vassal must go up every year to the overlord's land to appear before his lord; The vassal's yearly tribute in refined first-class gold is fixed and is to be weighed by the weights of the overlord's merchants; If the vassal writes to the enemy 'the troops of Hatti are coming to attack you; be on your guard', he has broken the oath; The great king lists the kings of equal rank to himself: the kings of Egypt, Babylonia, Hanigalbat or Assyria (and Ahhiyawa); Warriors come 'with a whole heart', 'not with a double heart', with one heart to make the king; The vassal may not excuse inaction by saying 'I am bound by oath and treaty; whether the enemy kills them or they kill him, I do not know'; A ruler who did not keep the treaty sworn by the gods is punished by them (defeat, death, abandonment); The vassal must take up the bow, stand with the king and fight his enemy wholeheartedly; The vassal must love the king and his friends and hate his enemy.

Only in Al-Mumtahana: no affection for God's enemies, Abraham's excellent example, examining emigrant women, and the women's pledge: Abraham and those with him are an excellent example: they declared themselves quit of their people and their gods, with enmity until they believe; Except Abraham's saying to his father 'I will ask forgiveness for you, though I have no power for you before God'; They despair of the hereafter as the unbelievers despair of those in the graves; Believers must not take God's enemies, who expelled the prophet, as allies (awliya') or secretly show them affection; Prohibition of killing one's children; Do not hold on to marriage ties with unbelieving women; dowries are reckoned between the communities; Believing women who emigrate are to be examined; if believers, they are not returned to the unbelievers, whose dowries are repaid; The women's pledge (bay'at al-nisa'): not to associate anything with God, steal, commit adultery, kill their children, bring a fabricated slander, or disobey in what is right; Abraham declares to his father and people that he is free of what they worship, except the one who created him; Dissolving marriages with women outside the community [divergence between the texts]; God does not forbid kindness and justice toward those who did not fight you over religion or expel you; Neither your blood-ties nor your children will benefit you on the Day of Resurrection; and 10 more.

matches.label: A submitting ruler's throne and gift are brought to a greater king [neutral]
matches.note: When Anitta comes against him, 'the man of Purušhanda brought me one throne of iron and one sceptre of iron' (W2:rev._74-75), and is brought to Neša and seated before the king in the inner chamber (rev._76-79). The queen of Sabaʾ sends Sulaymān a gift (27:35), which he scorns ('would you help me with wealth?', 27:36); her throne is brought to him instead (27:38-42), and she comes and submits (27:44). A ruler's throne and gift reach a greater king in token of submission; in Anitta the throne is the gift and is accepted, in the Quran the gift is refused and the throne is taken by a sign.

Only in Cyrus' titles, peace in Babylon, return of the gods and peoples (Cyrus Cylinder 20-36): The new king relieves the city's weariness and frees its people from an unfitting yoke; All the kings of the west (Amurru), from the upper to the lower sea, including those who live in tents, bring heavy tribute; The king asks the gods he has restored to speak daily before the chief god for his long life and good name; The king returns the deported statues of gods to their own cities and settles them in an eternal dwelling; The king traces his line through father and grandfather to a dynastic founder, 'eternal seed of kingship'; The deity promises that the king's son and grandson (and great-grandson) will exercise kingship; A royal inscription opens with a chain of titles (great king, mighty king, king of the world, king of Assyria, king of the four quarters, shepherd); Subject peoples or vassal kings come and kiss the king's feet in submission; The king is to rule from the rising to the setting of the sun, from the upper to the lower sea; The king is titled king of the four quarters of the world.

Only in The Doomed Prince: a son granted, three fates decreed, the prince shut away and set free: A parent tries to evade a child's foretold death by shutting him in a secluded house, which fails; Divine birth goddesses (the Hathors) come at a child's birth and pronounce his fate; A young prince leaves home with chariot, servant and dog to wander abroad as his heart desires, living by hunting; One whose death is decreed goes out of his house to meet it [divergence between the texts]; The hero refuses to have his own dog killed although it is one of his fates, because he raised it from a pup; A prince is fated to die by the crocodile, the snake or the dog; A childless king beseeches the god daily for an heir, citing his sacrifices and piety; 'If I fix a fate, who can alter it? If I speak, who can change it?'.

Only in Fighting for the oppressed; death in lofty towers: Fight for the oppressed men, women and children who cry 'take us out of this town of wrongdoers'; Whoever intercedes for good shares in it; whoever intercedes for evil bears a part of it; All comes from God; yet good befalling you is from God and evil from yourself; Were the Quran from other than God they would find much contradiction in it; When greeted, return a better greeting or the same; The plot of Satan is weak; Death will reach you wherever you are, even in lofty towers; 'I form light and create darkness, make peace and create evil (ra'); I YHWH do all these' [divergence between the texts]; The laggard thanks God he was absent when disaster struck, and wishes he had shared the spoil; Though they dig into Sheol or climb to heaven, hide on Carmel or at the bottom of the sea, God's hand will take them; People ordered to fight complain to God and wish to be spared the battle; Whatever word or news one hears is to be referred to the ruler (and those in authority), not concealed or spread [divergence between the texts]; and 4 more.

evidence.text: Read side by side in both originals (alignments/ane-quran/23-ane-quran.yaml).
Shared motifs, rarest first: The death or fate a man flees comes after him and meets him [divergence between the texts] (weight 7.7). Pair score 7.7.

Only in The Doomed Prince: the wife kills the snake, the dog and the crocodile pursue the prince: A crocodile in a lake and a water-being ('the Strong One') fight each other daily for months, each keeping the other in; Saved from danger, the hero offers to the sun god and praises his power every day; The fated agent itself speaks: 'I am your fate which has come after you'; 'Your god has given one of your fates into your hand': a danger overcome is credited to one's god; A wife keeps watch by her sleeping husband, makes the attacking snake drunk with beer and wine, and has it hacked to pieces; The hero refuses to have his own dog killed although it is one of his fates, because he raised it from a pup; A prince is fated to die by the crocodile, the snake or the dog.

Only in Al-Jumu'a: the messenger among the unlettered, the donkey carrying books, wishing for death, and the Friday prayer: When they saw trade or amusement they rushed to it and left the prophet standing; Those charged with the Torah who did not carry it are like a donkey carrying books (asfar); When the call to prayer is made on Friday (yawm al-jumu'a), hasten to God's remembrance and leave trading; after the prayer disperse and seek God's bounty; Challenge to the Jews: if you claim to be God's friends apart from others, wish for death, if you are truthful; they never will; The death you flee from will surely meet you; Israel likened to a donkey that knows, or does not understand, what it has [divergence between the texts]; Merchants ask when the new moon and sabbath will be over so they can sell grain with small ephah, big shekel and false scales; God raised among the unlettered (ummiyyun, Gentiles) a messenger from among them, reciting signs, purifying them and teaching the Book and wisdom; Reformer rebukes treading winepresses, loading donkeys and selling fish on the Sabbath; Trade on the weekly holy day [divergence between the texts]; The weekly holy day, and whether it rests on God's rest [divergence between the texts]; Litany of divine names: King, Holy, Peace, Faithful, Guardian, Mighty, Compeller, Proud, Creator, Maker, Fashioner; to him belong the most beautiful names; and 1 more.

matches.note: Byblos uses the report 'our lord is dead, Rib-Addi is dead: so (we are free) from his hand' to go over to Aziru while its ruler is away. 3:144 (Uhud, where the prophet was reported killed) asks the believers: 'if he dies or is killed, will you turn back on your heels?' matches.note: The king of Egypt as divine: Abimilki of Tyre writes a-na LUGAL EN-li₂-ia DINGIR.MEŠ-ia {d}UTU-ia 'to the king my lord, my gods, my Sun', the Sun who rises over the lands, who gives life by his sweet breath and thunders like Baddu (Baal); in 79:23-24 Pharaoh gathers and proclaims fa-qāla anā rabbukumu l-aʿlā. In the Amarna letters the vassal gives the title; in the Quran Pharaoh claims it for himself and is seized for it (79:25).

matches.label: Lordship that reaches from the rising to the setting of the sun
matches.note: The span from the rising to the setting of the sun belongs, in the Egyptian king's own letter, to the king, who is 'well like the sun in heaven' with his troops 'from sunrise to sunset' (ṣīt šamši adi ereb šamši). In 26:28 Moses answers Pharaoh's 'what is the Lord of the worlds?' with 'the Lord of the east and the west and what is between them'. The same title is taken from the king of Egypt and given to his challenger's Lord, and Pharaoh replies with a threat (26:29).

matches.note: A royal letter, opening with the sender's name ('thus says the king your lord' / 'it is from Sulaymān'), orders a ruler to come: 'come yourself, or send your son, and see the king' (alka attā šumma mārka šupur) against 'do not exalt yourselves against me and come to me in submission' (waʾtūnī muslimīn). matches.label: Slander or gossip pictured as eating
matches.note: Akkadian akālu karṣī 'to eat (someone's) pieces' is the ordinary idiom for slander: Labaya complains 'now they eat my pieces wrongfully' (yikalū karṣīya habālu-ma). Q 49:12 builds its ban on backbiting (ghība) on the same image, made literal and repellent: 'would one of you like to eat the flesh of his dead brother (an yaʾkula laḥma akhīhi maytan)?' In both slander of an absent man is eating his body.

matches.label: Slandering or backbiting someone is called eating him (his pieces, his flesh)
matches.note: Abdi-Heba: 'what have I done to the king my lord? they eat my pieces (i-ka-lu ka-ar-ṣi-ya), I am slandered before the king' (EA 286 o:5-7). Q 49:12 forbids backbiting (lā yaghtab) and pictures it as eating 'the flesh of his dead brother' (laḥma akhīhi maytan). The Akkadian idiom akālu karṣī ('eat the pieces' = slander, Aramaic ʾăkal qarṣîn) is made into an explicit image of eating a corpse.

matches.label: Who rules or commands the rising and the setting of the sun, in speech about a king
matches.note: The king of Egypt writes that 'Amun has put the upper land and the lower land, the rising of the sun and the setting of the sun, under the two feet of the king'. In 2:258 Ibrāhīm silences a king whom God had given kingship: 'God brings the sun from the east; so bring it from the west', and the king is confounded. In EA the god gives the sun's rising and setting to the king; in the Quran the king is challenged to command them and cannot.

Only in Erra in Esagil; Marduk recalls the flood when he left his throne (Erra I 124-162): After the flood the seven sages (apkallu) and master craftsmen were sent down to the Apsu and never brought up again; Dream of an immense tree whose top reaches heaven, visible to the ends of the earth, sheltering beasts and birds; The god's image is tarnished and must be cleansed by the fire god before the god returns to his seat; When the supreme god rises from his throne the seams of heaven and earth come apart: a flood follows, stars leave their places; People or offices that 'survived the flood' are named; A tree whose root reaches deep down and whose top reaches heaven; After the flood the seed of mankind is preserved and humanity rises again; A master craftsman skilled in every metal, stone, wood, dye and engraving; Waters pour both from the sky and from springs of the earth; Seven wisdoms (or seven sages/spirits of wisdom) attend the king or deity.

Only in The cleaving: the noble scribes: Over humans are guardians, noble scribes (kiraman katibin), who know what they do; The intercession of intercessors will not benefit the damned; no soul has power to help another; Then each soul will know what it has brought forward and what it left behind; At the end the graves are overturned and their contents scattered out (bu'thirat); At the end the seas are set aflame or burst forth (sujjirat, fujjirat); The people's deeds are written before God, who will repay them into their bosom; At the end the sky is split, cleft or opened (infatarat, inshaqqat, furijat); Stars and constellations (kesilim) give no light, the sun is dark at its rising and the moon does not shine; God formed the kidneys and wove (knit) the speaker in his mother's womb; A written record (tablet [divergence between the texts]; Rhetorical formula 'And what will make you know what X is?' (wa ma adraka ma) introducing an eschatological term; God keeps a book in which names are written and from which sinners are blotted.

Only in The Seven goad Erra: the field is better than the city (Erra I 45-91): The open field is praised over city life: city bread cannot compare with a cake baked in embers, the palace with a shepherd's hut; Neglected weapons: cobwebs on the war gear, the bow too stiff, the arrowhead dull, the sword rusted for lack of slaughter; In a primeval or ideal land the lion does not kill and the wolf does not carry off the lamb; A warrior god lies idle in bed with his wife and is goaded by his weapons and companions to go out to war; Destruction motivated by human noise or overpopulation; Nations will beat swords into plowshares and spears into pruning hooks and learn war no more.

Only in David's thanksgiving psalm (composite of Pss 105, 96, 106): A psalm sung in the narrative is stitched from passages found in the Psalter; Prayer: 'save us, gather us and deliver us from the nations'; The patriarchs few in number wander from nation to nation, protected by God; All the people say 'Amen' and praise YHWH; 'Touch not my anointed ones, do my prophets no harm'; The world is firmly established and cannot be moved; Hymn recalls God's covenant with Abraham, oath to Isaac and statute to Jacob for a thousand generations; God comes to judge the earth with righteousness, and all creation rejoices; Proclamation among the nations: 'YHWH is king' (YHWH malakh); Idols called 'elilim' ('nothings'); YHWH is great and to be feared above all gods; Refrain 'Give thanks to YHWH for he is good, for his steadfast love is forever'.

matches.note: libbi abiya ša lā ilāni uzennû ittiya šaplānu libbašu rēma rašīšuma 'they turned my father's heart against me, against the gods' will, but deep down his heart had pity on me' ~ uqtulū yūsufa ... yakhlu lakum wajhu abīkum 'so that your father's face will be yours alone' (12:9). The brothers aim at the father's favour on both sides; in Assur they manage to estrange him, though he still pities the son in secret, while in the Quran they plan to win it for themselves by getting rid of Joseph. Only in Cimmerians, Hilakku, Mannea, Bīt-Dakkūri and Gambulu (Esarhaddon 1 iii 43-83): The king returns to the citizens of the holy city the fields a robber chieftain had seized; The Cimmerians (Gimirrāya, Gomer), a horde from far away, are fought; Struck by terror, a chieftain brings tribute of animals to the king and kisses his feet; the king has mercy on him; Conquered population deported to Assyria or another distant land.

Only in The pacified Delta and the wretched Asiatic, a crocodile on its bank (Instruction for Merikare): The old king tells how he pacified the west and settled the eastern border with towns of choice people to repel foreigners; Because the revenues of the north are in the king's hand, a failure of the Nile flood will not distress him; The king had the Asiatics struck, their people captured and their cattle seized until they abhorred Egypt; The Asiatic nomad is wretched: his land is short of water and wood, he never settles, fights 'since the time of Horus', neither wins nor is defeated, a crocodile on its bank.

matches.label: A god-empowered king goes, or rules, from the place of the sun's rising to the place of its setting
matches.note: ina tukultišunu rabīti ištu ṣīt šamši adi ereb šamši šalṭiš attallakuma 'trusting in them (the gods) I went about triumphantly from the sunrise to the sunset' ~ innā makkannā lahu fī l-arḍ (18:84) ... ḥattā idhā balagha maghriba sh-shams (18:86) ... balagha maṭliʿa sh-shams (18:90). The same pair of words for where the sun rises and where it sets (ṣīt šamši / maṭliʿ ash-shams; ereb šamši / maghrib ash-shams) marks the range of a king the divine power has made strong. The order is reversed: the Assyrian goes from rising to setting, Dhū l-Qarnayn goes west first.

evidence.text: Read side by side in both originals (alignments/ane-quran/15-ane-quran.yaml).
Shared motifs, rarest first: A god-empowered king goes, or rules, from the place of the sun's rising to the place of its setting (weight 7.3). Pair score 7.3.

Only in Esarhaddon's titles, the restorer of the gods, and the gifts of the gods (Esarhaddon 1 ii 12-39): The king returns the deported statues of gods to their own cities and settles them in an eternal dwelling; The king traces his line through father and grandfather to a dynastic founder, 'eternal seed of kingship'; A royal inscription opens with a chain of titles (great king, mighty king, king of the world, king of Assyria, king of the four quarters, shepherd); Each of the great gods in turn bestows a gift on the king (crown, heroism, abundance, justice ...); The king is to rule from the rising to the setting of the sun, from the upper to the lower sea.

Only in Dhul-Qarnayn, the setting and rising sun, and the barrier against Gog and Magog (Surah 18:83-101): When God's promise comes the barrier is leveled to the ground; The conqueror is given the choice to punish the people at the sunset or treat them kindly; A people complain that Gog and Magog spread corruption in the land; A barrier of iron blocks filling the gap between two cliffs, heated with bellows and sealed with molten copper, shuts out Gog and Magog; At the sun's rising the conqueror finds a people with no shelter from it; Between two mountain barriers the conqueror finds a people who scarcely understand speech; At the end peoples surge into one another like waves; At the place of sunset the conqueror finds the sun setting in a muddy (or hot) spring; The people offer tribute for a barrier; the conqueror declines payment and asks for their labor; A ruler builds a barrier across the gap between two mountains to cut off invading peoples; A ruler builds a barrier across the gap between two mountains to cut off invading peoples [divergence between the texts]; Whether a king's barrier against invaders holds or is breached [divergence between the texts]; and 16 more.

Only in Hymn to Enki, the meš tree of the abzu who regulates the calendar and makes the land fertile (Enki and the world order): At the god's word or approach flocks give birth, fields yield and stores are heaped; A god or king is likened to a great tree planted in the deep whose shade covers heaven and earth; A god counts the days, sets the months in their houses and completes the years (regulates the calendar); God called the patriarch's shepherd all his life.

Only in The wise Book, creation, sun and moon, the prayer of paradise: Sun and moon are set to rule day and night and mark signs and seasons [divergence between the texts]; The blessed in paradise cry 'Glory to you, O God', greet with 'Peace' and end with 'Praise be to God, Lord of the worlds'; The damned are given a drink of boiling water (hamim); God made the sun a radiance and the moon a light with measured stations, to count years and reckoning; People marvel that a reminder came through a man from among them; Creation is completed in six days [divergence between the texts]; God originates creation and then repeats it (resurrection as re-creation); Opponents call the prophet or his message 'manifest sorcery'; Creation is completed in six days; After creating the heavens and earth God established himself on the Throne (istawa 'ala l-'arsh); Intercession avails only for whom God permits; Paradise as gardens (of ʿAdn) beneath which rivers flow, where the righteous abide forever; and 1 more.

matches.label: A god sends or instructs a raven, which works the ground as a man would
matches.note: uga(mušen) / ghurāb. A raven works the ground at a god's command and does what men do: in the Sumerian it plants and pollinates the first date palm and works the shadouf ('a bird like the raven doing the work of man - who had ever seen such a thing?'); in 5:31 it shows Adam's son how to cover his brother's body, and he says yā waylatā a-ʿajaztu an akūna mithla hādhā l-ghurāb.

Only in Inana goes up into the mountains; Enki's raven plants the first date palm (Inana and Šu-kale-tuda 1-90): A god gives instructions to a bird (the raven), which then performs the work of a man; The raven plants, climbs and pollinates the first date palm and works the shadouf, an origin of date cultivation; A deity abandons heaven, earth and a list of named temples to go elsewhere (into the mountains or the underworld); A narrative refrain punctuates the story: 'What did one say to another? Only in Dumuzid's flight as a snake, Inana's grief, the fly, and the half-year decree (Inana's descent 359-412): Two siblings each spend half the year in the underworld, one released when the other is taken; An animal (a fly) reveals where the hidden man is and is rewarded by the deity with a decreed destiny; A goddess weeps bitterly for her lost husband, tears out her hair and asks 'Where is my man?'; A decree is followed by the formula 'and so it was / it truly became so' (ur5 he2-en-na-nam); Underworld demons eat no food or offering, know no marital love or children, snatch wife from husband, son from knee, bride from her in-laws' house; A pursued man prays to the sun god, who turns his hands and feet into a snake's so he can escape the demons; A composition ends with a doxology to its deity: 'praise of X is sweet / magnificent' (za3-mi2).

Only in Solomon, the speech of birds, the ants, the hoopoe and the Queen of Sheba: Entering Solomon's palace, the queen takes its floor of smooth glass for a pool and bares her legs; The hoopoe returns with sure news from Sabaʾ, knowledge Solomon lacked; Solomon sends the hoopoe to drop his letter before the queen and wait for their reply; Solomon reviews the birds, finds the hoopoe absent and threatens to punish or slaughter it unless it brings a clear excuse; An ʿifrīt of the jinn offers to bring the queen's throne before Solomon rises from his seat; Solomon's letter begins 'In the name of God, the Merciful, the Compassionate' and demands submission; The queen sends a gift to see what the envoys bring back; Solomon rejects the wealth and threatens invasion; The queen confesses she wronged herself and submits with Solomon to God, Lord of the worlds; Solomon has the queen's throne disguised to test whether she recognizes it; she says 'It is as though it were it'; The queen and her people prostrate to the sun instead of God; Solomon inherits from David (knowledge and kingship); Solomon prays to be inspired to thank God for favor to him and his parents and to be admitted among the righteous; and 42 more.

Shared motifs, rarest first: The netherworld (hell) has seven gates (weight 6.8); The underworld has seven gates, bolted and opened one at a time (weight 5.8). Pair score 12.6.

Only in Inana passes the seven gates, is stripped, judged and hung on a hook (Inana's descent 68-172): The slain body is turned into a corpse and hung on a hook (peg) on the wall; At the gate of the netherworld the gatekeepers question those who arrive [divergence between the texts]; Before a perilous journey the deity instructs a faithful minister what to do if she does not return; The arriving goddess makes her sister rise from the throne and sits on it herself; Seven underworld judges give their verdict: their look is the look of death, their word the word of anger, their shout the shout of guilt; At each underworld gate one ornament or garment is removed until the goddess arrives naked; A figure slaps his or her thigh in dismay or grief on hearing bad news; Arriving at a closed house or gate, a deity calls out to the doorkeeper by name: 'Open the house, open!'; Death or Sheol has gates (sha'arei mavet); Like a vanishing cloud, whoever goes down to Sheol does not come up; his place knows him no more; The underworld is the land of no return, the road whose traveller never comes back.

Only in Ninĝišzida's journey: the sister asks why the demon takes him; the nether world gives no water, flour or wool; she offers her jewels: The doomed god likens himself to a canal his mother dug that now gives no water, a tamarisk without shade, a date palm whose fruit no one enjoys; In the nether world the river gives no water to drink, the field no flour, the sheep no wool; What the dead are given to eat and drink in the other world [divergence between the texts]; The captured foe is haltered like a wild bull and bound at the elbows.

Only in Muhammad: deeds nullified, striking necks and freeing captives, and the four rivers of the Garden: The damned are given boiling water to drink which tears their bowels apart; The Garden has rivers of unstaling water, of milk unchanged in taste, of wine delightful to drinkers, and of purified honey; Some listen to the prophet and on leaving ask the learned 'What did he say just now?'; God has sealed their hearts; Those killed in God's way: their deeds are not lost; he guides them and admits them to a Garden he has made known to them; The signs/portents (ashrat) of the Hour have already come; The prophet is told to ask forgiveness for his own sin and for the believing men and women; In battle, strike the necks of unbelievers; when they are subdued bind them, then free them as favor or for ransom until war lays down its burdens; People eat as sheep or cattle eat; Four rivers in the Garden [divergence between the texts]; If you help God he will help you and make your feet firm; The Hour will come upon them suddenly while they are unaware; Whether a bound captive is released or killed [contrast between the texts]; and 14 more.

Enki recalls that after the flood only Zi-ud-sura 'although a human' (nam-lu2-ulu3) stayed alive, and then the gods swore that no human would live (nu-mu-til3) again; they then ask whether Gilgameš, son of a goddess, might escape. 21:34-35: 'We have not given any human (bashar) before you everlasting life (al-khuld): if you die, will they be everlasting?' and 'every soul tastes death'. Sumerian names one exception and debates a second; the Quran admits none.

evidence.text: Shared motifs, rarest first: A king exhausts the young men of his city with incessant games or labour (weight 7.7). Pair score 7.7.

Only in The ball game oppresses the young men; the widows' outcry sends ball and mallet to the nether world: A hero weeps aloud over a beloved lost possession; Mothers bring bread and sisters pour water for the worn-out young men; A king praises himself without ceasing; A hero's prized object falls into the netherworld beyond his reach; Lament: 'Who will go down and bring it up for me from the netherworld?'; The gate of the netherworld (Ganzer) where the living may sit and lament; God hears the cry of the oppressed widow and orphan and punishes measure for measure.

Only in Gilgameš oppresses Uruk; the gods hear and Aruru creates Enkidu from clay (Gilgameš SB I): The gods create a rival equal to the overbearing hero, so that they contend and the city may have rest; The oppressed people's complaint about their king reaches the gods, who act on it; The tyrant king lets no girl go free to her bridegroom (claims the bride before the husband); Ishmael foretold to be a wild ass of a man, his hand against all; A wild man, hairy and naked, eats grass with the gazelles and drinks at the water-hole with the herds; A hunter or trapper encounters the wild man at the animals' water-hole and is terrified; The speaker too was 'pinched off from clay' (qoratsti), like a figure nipped from a lump of clay; A god fashions a creature from clay to serve his purpose; A deity chooses the ruler, 'the true shepherd', in the divine assembly for his attractiveness or worth; First human shaped from dust, clay or soil.

Only in Enkidu's report (recension 5.B) and the transition to the search for life: The man who exalted himself bows like an ox while worms eat him below; Grief over death drives a king to set out in search of life; A man burned to death has no ghost in the netherworld; his smoke went up to the sky; Stillborn children play at a table of gold and silver with honey and ghee in the netherworld; Person with skin disease lives alone outside the camp.

Only in 'Tell me the order of the Netherworld': the fates of the dead (Gilgameš SB XII): The living hero embraces and kisses the ghost of his friend and begs: 'tell me the order of the netherworld'; The body once delighted in is devoured by grubs like an old beam and filled with dust like a crack in the ground; The ghost hesitates: 'I cannot tell you; if I tell you, sit down and weep'; The ghost of one whose corpse lies in the open country finds no rest in the netherworld; One who died (properly) lies on the bed of the gods in the netherworld; A returned spirit tells the living the order (rules) of the netherworld; The body once loved is infested by vermin like an old garment and filled with dust; Mourners cry 'woe' and throw themselves prostrate in the dust; The man fallen in battle has no father and mother to hold his head; his wife weeps; The ghost who has no one to make funerary offerings eats scraps tossed in the street.

matches.note: The household as a reason not to march: Gilgameš proclaims by horn 'whoever has a household, to his household; whoever has a mother, to his mother' and takes only unattached men (nitaḫ saĝ-dili). matches.label: The modes in which a deity speaks with a human: dream, waking speech, revelation, veil, messenger
matches.note: Ranked modes of divine speech to a man: En-suḫgir-ana boasts 'he may see dreams with Inana at night, but I converse (inim bal) with Inana awake'. 42:51 lists the only three ways God speaks to a human: waḥy, from behind a veil, or by a messenger. Sumerian puts waking conversation above the dream; the Quran allows no unmediated speech.

matches.note: Gudea's justice: in a house with no son (ibila, heir) the daughter becomes heir (Cyl. matches.note: Ningal weeps before An and begs Enlil 'let my city not be destroyed, let its people not perish', twice, in the assembly; 'An did not turn back (gur) his word, Enlil did not soothe my heart'. Abraham 'disputes with us about the people of Lot' and is told 'turn from this; your Lord's command has come; there comes upon them a punishment ghayru mardūd' (not to be turned back). The goddess pleads for her own city and is overruled by her superiors; the prophet pleads for another's people and is praised as ḥalīm awwāh munīb.

Only in The great cedar of Eden felled and sent down to Sheol: The trees of Eden already in the netherworld are comforted when the great tree descends to join them; No tree in the garden of God, Eden, equalled the great tree's beauty; all the trees of Eden envied it; Assyria/Pharaoh as a towering cedar of Lebanon nourished by the deep (tehom), its top among the clouds, all birds nesting and beasts bearing young under it, all nations in its shade; God brings low the high tree and exalts the low tree, dries up the green tree and makes the dry tree flourish; The fallen king lies in the netherworld among the uncircumcised and those slain by the sword; Because it grew proud of its height, foreigners cut the great tree down; its boughs fall on mountains and valleys and the peoples leave its shade; Birds of every wing nest in the branches and shade of a great tree (kingdom); If God is silent the speaker will be like those who go down to the Pit (bor); God plants a garden (Eden) in the east and places the first human there; Oracle or vision dated by year, month and day of the exile of King Jehoiachin.

evidence.text: Shared motifs, rarest first: Lament that God has spurned his anointed, defiled his crown and cast his throne to the ground (weight 7.7). Pair score 7.7.

Only in City by city the gods depart and the goddesses weep (Sumer and Urim 115-224): The en-priest(ess) is snatched from the Ĝipar shrine and carried off to enemy territory; A city or land is poured out 'like milk to the dogs'; God makes the sufferer dwell in darkness like those long dead; The god himself sends a fierce foreign people against his own city or people; Rachel weeps in Ramah for her children and refuses to be comforted; A goddess flees her temple like a pigeon flying from the window; Ruined city never reinhabited, even by Arab tents or shepherds; inhabited by desert creatures, ostriches, jackals and dancing goat-demons (se'irim); The city's goddess weeps bitterly: 'Alas, the destroyed city, my destroyed house'; The chief god himself brings down a foreign people (Gutians, Elamites) from the mountains to destroy his land; Desert creatures or demons (tsiyyim, iyyim) and ostriches inhabit the ruined city; Destruction undoes fertility: brackish water in rivers, weeds in fields, no lambs in the fold, no churning song; City after city its god 'takes an unfamiliar path' away from his beloved dwelling and abandons it; and 2 more.

Only in Psalm 89, Ethan's hymn of the divine council, Rahab crushed, and the broken Davidic covenant: The king calls God 'my father' and God makes him firstborn, highest of the kings of earth; God sets the king's hand on the Sea and his right hand on the Rivers; The dynasty will be established like the moon, a faithful witness in the sky; If the king's sons sin they will be punished with the rod, but God's love will not be withdrawn; God created Zaphon (north) and Yamin (south); Tabor and Hermon sing his name; God stills the roaring of the seas and the tumult of the peoples; Righteousness and justice are the foundation of God's throne; love and truth go before him; The king (or his name, dynasty, throne) will endure as long as the sun and moon; If there were other gods they would seek a way to the Lord of the Throne; God crushed Rahab like a corpse and scattered his enemies; God gives strength to his king and exalts the horn of his anointed (messiah); Prophet anoints the chosen king with a horn of oil among his brothers; the spirit comes on him; and 15 more.

Only in City by city the gods depart and the goddesses weep (Sumer and Urim 115-224): The en-priest(ess) is snatched from the Ĝipar shrine and carried off to enemy territory; A city or land is poured out 'like milk to the dogs'; God makes the sufferer dwell in darkness like those long dead; Rachel weeps in Ramah for her children and refuses to be comforted; Lament that God has spurned his anointed, defiled his crown and cast his throne to the ground; A goddess flees her temple like a pigeon flying from the window; Ruined city never reinhabited, even by Arab tents or shepherds; inhabited by desert creatures, ostriches, jackals and dancing goat-demons (se'irim); The city's goddess weeps bitterly: 'Alas, the destroyed city, my destroyed house'; The chief god himself brings down a foreign people (Gutians, Elamites) from the mountains to destroy his land; Desert creatures or demons (tsiyyim, iyyim) and ostriches inhabit the ruined city; Destruction undoes fertility: brackish water in rivers, weeds in fields, no lambs in the fold, no churning song; City after city its god 'takes an unfamiliar path' away from his beloved dwelling and abandons it; and 1 more.

Only in The Night Journey and the two corruptions of the Children of Israel (Surah 17:1-8): Israel addressed as descendants of those carried with Noah, who was a grateful servant; Divine warning 'if you return (to sin), we will return (to punishment)'; It is decreed in the Book that Israel will work corruption on earth twice; God takes his servant on a journey to show him some of his signs; The storm or enemy destroys the city a second time; The enemy sent against the city enters its sanctuary and wrecks what it finds; The god himself rouses a mighty foreign enemy against his own land or people; God sends against Israel servants of his of great might who range through their homes; Because of his people's offence their own god lets a foreign power oppress them for a time, and later gives the land (or the upper hand) back; A swift journey by night ends at a distant sanctuary; God carried his servant by night from the Sacred Mosque to the Farthest Mosque; After the first punishment God restores Israel's turn with wealth and sons; and 5 more.

Only in Complaint of the young men to Enki; Urim besieged; the queen led into slavery (Sumer and Urim 225-284): She who was a princess among provinces has become a forced laborer; Zion's precious sons, worth fine gold, now counted as clay pots; Lament cry: 'Why, YHWH, do you stand far off and hide in times of trouble?'; The city's goddess weeps bitterly: 'Alas, the destroyed city, my destroyed house'; Famine becomes severe in the besieged city; there is no bread; The chief god himself brings down a foreign people (Gutians, Elamites) from the mountains to destroy his land; The ruined city, personified as a woman, speaks in the first person; City after city its god 'takes an unfamiliar path' away from his beloved dwelling and abandons it.

Only in Mystical cultic commentary: Ištar weeps for her brother, the flayed god, Orion, Dumuzi (Q009249, SAA 3): A god's body parts are equated one by one with plants, trees and substances (tamarisk his tuft, cedar his knee, myrrh his moisture ...); A child or heir is hidden away (by parents or goddesses) to protect him from a killer; Rites of the month Tammuz: day of lamentation, Dumuzi is questioned and goes up, roasted grain cast on him; A defeated god is bound and flayed; his skin is put on a constellation (Orion) and his body handed to the Anunnaki; A goddess weeps and wails for her slain brother god and sees his body, its blood flowing to the earth; Colophon: the secret of the great gods; the knowing may show it to the knowing, the unknowing may not see it, taboo of the great gods; The victorious god treads on the neck of his insubmissive enemy; The dying god's sister (Belili / Geshtinanna) hears the wailing for her brother and cries 'Do not rob me of my only brother!'; A cultic commentary explains each ritual act or object of a festival as an episode of a myth ('the X which ... is the Y'); The warrior god (Ninurta, or Nabû in commentary) defeats and kills the Anzu bird.

(1:11) כָּל עַמָּ֤הּ נֶאֱנָחִים֙ מְבַקְּשִׁ֣ים לֶ֔חֶם נָתְנ֧וּ מחמודיהם מַחֲמַדֵּיהֶ֛ם בְּאֹ֖כֶל לְהָשִׁ֣יב נָ֑פֶשׁ רְאֵ֤ה יְהוָה֙ וְֽהַבִּ֔יטָה כִּ֥י הָיִ֖יתִי זוֹלֵלָֽה (1:12) ל֣וֹא אֲלֵיכֶם֮ כָּל עֹ֣בְרֵי דֶרֶךְ֒ הַבִּ֣יטוּ וּרְא֗וּ אִם יֵ֤שׁ מַכְאוֹב֙ כְּמַכְאֹבִ֔י אֲשֶׁ֥ר עוֹלַ֖ל לִ֑י אֲשֶׁר֙ הוֹגָ֣ה יְהוָ֔ה בְּי֖וֹם חֲר֥וֹן אַפּֽוֹ (1:13) מִמָּר֛וֹם שָֽׁלַח אֵ֥שׁ בְּעַצְמֹתַ֖י וַיִּרְדֶּ֑נָּה פָּרַ֨שׂ רֶ֤שֶׁת לְרַגְלַי֙ הֱשִׁיבַ֣נִי אָח֔וֹר נְתָנַ֨נִי֙ שֹֽׁמֵמָ֔ה כָּל הַיּ֖וֹם דָּוָֽה (1:14) נִשְׂקַד֩ עֹ֨ל פְּשָׁעַ֜י בְּיָד֗וֹ יִשְׂתָּֽרְג֛וּ עָל֥וּ עַל צַוָּארִ֖י הִכְשִׁ֣יל כֹּחִ֑י נְתָנַ֣נִי אֲדֹנָ֔י בִּידֵ֖י לֹא אוּכַ֥ל קֽוּם (1:15) סִלָּ֨ה כָל אַבִּירַ֤י אֲדֹנָי֙ בְּקִרְבִּ֔י קָרָ֥א עָלַ֛י מוֹעֵ֖ד לִשְׁבֹּ֣ר בַּחוּרָ֑י גַּ֚ת דָּרַ֣ךְ אֲדֹנָ֔י לִבְתוּלַ֖ת בַּת יְהוּדָֽה (1:16) עַל אֵ֣לֶּה אֲנִ֣י בוֹכִיָּ֗ה עֵינִ֤י עֵינִי֙ יֹ֣רְדָה מַּ֔יִם כִּֽי רָחַ֥ק מִמֶּ֛נִּי מְנַחֵ֖ם מֵשִׁ֣יב נַפְשִׁ֑י הָי֤וּ בָנַי֙ שֽׁוֹמֵמִ֔ים כִּ֥י גָבַ֖ר אוֹיֵֽב (1:17) פֵּֽרְשָׂ֨ה צִיּ֜וֹן בְּיָדֶ֗יהָ אֵ֤ין מְנַחֵם֙ לָ֔הּ צִוָּ֧ה יְהוָ֛ה לְיַעֲקֹ֖ב סְבִיבָ֣יו צָרָ֑יו הָיְתָ֧ה יְרוּשָׁלִַ֛ם לְנִדָּ֖ה בֵּינֵיהֶֽם (1:18) צַדִּ֥יק ה֛וּא יְהוָ֖ה כִּ֣י פִ֣יהוּ מָרִ֑יתִי שִׁמְעוּ נָ֣א כָל עמים הָֽעַמִּ֗ים וּרְאוּ֙ מַכְאֹבִ֔י בְּתוּלֹתַ֥י וּבַחוּרַ֖י הָלְכ֥וּ בַשֶּֽׁבִי (1:19) קָרָ֤אתִי לַֽמְאַהֲבַי֙ הֵ֣מָּה רִמּ֔וּנִי כֹּהֲנַ֥י וּזְקֵנַ֖י בָּעִ֣יר גָּוָ֑עוּ כִּֽי בִקְשׁ֥וּ אֹ֨כֶל֙ לָ֔מוֹ וְיָשִׁ֖יבוּ אֶת נַפְשָֽׁם (1:20) רְאֵ֨ה יְהוָ֤ה כִּֽי צַר לִי֙ מֵעַ֣י חֳמַרְמָ֔רוּ נֶהְפַּ֤ךְ לִבִּי֙ בְּקִרְבִּ֔י כִּ֥י מָר֖וֹ מָרִ֑יתִי מִח֥וּץ שִׁכְּלָה חֶ֖רֶב בַּבַּ֥יִת כַּמָּֽוֶת (1:21) שָׁמְע֞וּ כִּ֧י נֶאֱנָחָ֣ה אָ֗נִי אֵ֤ין מְנַחֵם֙ לִ֔י כָּל אֹ֨יְבַ֜י שָׁמְע֤וּ רָֽעָתִי֙ שָׂ֔שׂוּ כִּ֥י אַתָּ֖ה עָשִׂ֑יתָ הֵבֵ֥אתָ יוֹם קָרָ֖אתָ וְיִֽהְי֥וּ כָמֽוֹנִי (1:22) תָּבֹ֨א כָל רָעָתָ֤ם לְפָנֶ֨יךָ֙ וְעוֹלֵ֣ל לָ֔מוֹ כַּאֲשֶׁ֥ר עוֹלַ֛לְתָּ לִ֖י עַ֣ל כָּל פְּשָׁעָ֑י כִּֽי רַבּ֥וֹת אַנְחֹתַ֖י וְלִבִּ֥י דַוָּֽי

evidence.text: Shared motifs, rarest first: She who was a princess among provinces has become a forced laborer (weight 7.7); The ruined city, personified as a woman, speaks in the first person (weight 6.6). Pair score 14.4.

Only in Complaint of the young men to Enki; Urim besieged; the queen led into slavery (Sumer and Urim 225-284): A god leaves his city like a prisoner of war, his hands fettered; Zion's precious sons, worth fine gold, now counted as clay pots; Lament cry: 'Why, YHWH, do you stand far off and hide in times of trouble?'; The city's goddess weeps bitterly: 'Alas, the destroyed city, my destroyed house'; Famine becomes severe in the besieged city; there is no bread; The chief god himself brings down a foreign people (Gutians, Elamites) from the mountains to destroy his land; City after city its god 'takes an unfamiliar path' away from his beloved dwelling and abandons it.

Only in Lamentations 1: 'How lonely sits the city', Zion as a widow with no comforter: The fallen city is likened to a menstruant (niddah) whose impurity is in her skirts; The ruined city sits alone like a widow; From on high God sent fire into the sufferer's bones; God spread a net for the sufferer's feet and turned him back; The Lord trod the virgin daughter of Judah as in a winepress; 'Is it nothing to you, all who pass by? Look and see if there is any sorrow like my sorrow'; Refrain that the city has no one to comfort her; The princes became like deer that find no pasture and flee without strength; The sufferer confesses 'YHWH is righteous, for I rebelled against his word'; The starving people trade their treasures for food to keep alive; The yoke of the sinner's transgressions is knotted by God's hand onto her neck; The sufferer's bowels churn and heart turns over within her; and 9 more.

Only in The locust plague and the call to lament: Even the beasts of the field long for / cry out to God in the drought; Successive kinds of locust (gazam, arbeh, yeleq, hasil) each eat what the previous one left; Invading horde (locusts) has the teeth of a lion and fangs of a lioness; Tell this to your children, and they to theirs, and theirs to the next generation; Lament like a virgin in sackcloth for the husband of her youth; Proclaim a fast, call a solemn assembly, gather elders and all the people to the house of God and cry out; Prayer accompanied by fasting, sackcloth and ashes; The Day of YHWH is near: a day of cloud, a time of doom for the nations; Because of sin the land mourns and beasts, birds and even fish of the sea perish; Locusts brought by an east wind devour all vegetation left after the hail.

matches.label: The reason given for the god's handing his own city over to destruction
matches.note: The motive differs. Enlil gives no sin as the reason for Urim's fall: its reign 'had been long indeed but had to exhaust itself' (G:366-369), and other laments of this group ask what the people did to deserve it. In 17:4-5 the destruction was decreed in the Book because 'you will make mischief in the land twice (la-tufsidunna ... marratayn)', and 17:7-8 ties each army to their own wrongdoing ('if you do evil, it is against yourselves').

matches.note: Enlil's answer to Nanna: 'Urim was indeed given kingship (nam-lugal) but it was not given an eternal reign (bal da-ri2); who has ever seen a reign of kingship that would take precedence for ever?' (G:366-369). 3:26: 'O God, owner of kingship (mālik al-mulk), you give kingship (al-mulk) to whom you will and take kingship from whom you will.' Both name the thing given and withdrawn as kingship; the Sumerian adds that every reign's turn (bal) must run out.

matches.label: 'Who can change the word that has gone out?' / 'none can change his words'
matches.note: The same refusal formula in the same setting, a plea before the highest judge: 'the judgment of the assembly cannot be turned back, the word spoken by An and Enlil knows no overturning (šu bal-e nu-zu)' (G:364-365); 'do not dispute before me ... the word is not changed before me (mā yubaddalu l-qawlu ladayya), and I am not unjust to the servants' (50:28-29). The Sumerian word is the council's; the Quranic one is the warning already sent (qaddamtu ilaykum bi-l-waʿīd).

Only in Lamentations 1: 'How lonely sits the city', Zion as a widow with no comforter: The fallen city is likened to a menstruant (niddah) whose impurity is in her skirts; The ruined city sits alone like a widow; From on high God sent fire into the sufferer's bones; God spread a net for the sufferer's feet and turned him back; The Lord trod the virgin daughter of Judah as in a winepress; 'Is it nothing to you, all who pass by? matches.label: Whether a decreed term or fate can be altered after it is fixed
matches.note: Both texts allow that a fixed fate can be changed by the god who fixed it. In the Death of Ur-Namma An 'altered his holy word' and Enlil 'deceitfully (šu lul) changed the fate he had decreed', so the king dies early and the gods lament (1:8-14). In 13:38-39 'every term has a writing (li-kulli ajalin kitāb); God effaces what he wills and confirms, and with him is the Mother of the Book': the same power, stated as sovereign right, not as betrayal.

Only in Disaster strikes Urim and the gods mourn the death of the shepherd Ur-Namma (Death of Ur-Namma): The high gods alter their holy word and 'deceitfully' change the fate they had decreed for the king; At the king's death the gods mourn: a goddess laments, Enki shuts his door and lies fasting, the moon god frowns, the sun does not rise; Evil comes upon the city and makes the trustworthy shepherd-king pass away; After the king's death the canals, barley and pastures fail and the land grows 'grass of mourning'; All Israel gathers to lament a dead leader; The divine mother of the king weeps 'Oh my heart!' for her son in the public square; A god in grief wails and lies down fasting; In the catastrophe the sun god sets and does not rise again.

matches.label: The dead cannot go back to the life they left
matches.note: Ur-Namma, with no god to help him, says 'just as the rain pouring down from heaven cannot turn back, alas, nor can I turn back to brick-built Urim' (1:164-165). The dying man of 23:99-100 asks 'my Lord, send me back, that I may do right in what I left', and is refused: 'no! ... and behind them is a barrier (barzakh) until the day they are raised'. Ur-Namma wants to go back to his city; the Quranic man wants to go back to do good. Both are refused; in the Quran the refusal lasts only until the resurrection.

matches.label: The dead man laments what he did not do or enjoy in life
matches.note: The dead man's regret, in the first person: Ur-Namma weeps that he could not finish the wall of Urim, enjoy his new palace, embrace his wife or raise his sons on his knees (1:148-153). In 89:23-24, on the day hell is brought near, man remembers 'and he says: would that I had sent ahead (qaddamtu) for my life'. The Sumerian king regrets the life he did not get to enjoy; the Quranic man regrets the good he did not send ahead.

units.title: A tigi to Enlil for Ur-Namma, builder of the E-kur
Pharaoh, 'no god but me', Haman's tower of fired brick, and the drowning

matches.label: A ruler has bricks made for a lofty building that reaches up to heaven
matches.note: A king's brickwork reaching for heaven: Ur-Namma 'prepared the brick mould' (giš-u3-šub, A:13) and 'made the lofty E-kur grow towards heaven (an-še3) in Dur-an-ki' (A:20) because Enlil told him to. Pharaoh orders 'kindle a fire for me on the clay, Haman, and make me a tower, so that I may look up to the God of Moses' (28:38): fired brick, a tower to heaven, built in defiance of God. Same building technique and aim, opposite relation to the god.

matches.note: A king says no one after him will have what he has: Šulgi, at the end of his hymn, claims that from the time the seed of mankind came forth to its full flourishing no king will equal what he achieved (332-336). evidence.text: Read side by side in both originals (alignments/ane-quran/03-ane-quran.yaml).

Shared motifs, rarest first: No mortal goes up to heaven (weight 7.7); Who has gone up to heaven and come down, gathered the wind in his fists, wrapped the waters in a garment? What is his name and his son's name? (weight 7.1). Pair score 14.8.

Only in Šulgi's service to the gods, preservation of old hymns, and charge to a future king (Šulgi B): The king claims never to have done violence to another king, Akkadian, Sumerian or Gutian; The king collected and preserved old hymns from ancient times, never declaring them false, and added them to the singers' repertoire; 'Whatever is acquired is destined to be lost; what mortal has ever reached the heavens?'; The king releases water into canals and makes trees grow on their banks; The gods' hunger and thirst (their offerings) are the king's greatest concern; A future king is enjoined to honour the present king's name and keep his songs; The king does justice and righteousness for all his people.

Only in Near compromise, prayer times, the praised station, the spirit, the challenge and the demanded signs (Surah 17:73-100): Were angels walking the earth, God would have sent them an angel as messenger; The creator of heavens and earth is able to create the like of them (resurrection argument); The astray are gathered on their faces, blind, dumb and deaf; Opponents demand a spring gushing from the earth or a garden of palms and vines with rivers; Opponents demand that the prophet have a house of gold ornament; Opponents demand that the sky fall on them in pieces or God and the angels appear; Whenever the fire of hell abates, God increases its blaze; Even owning the treasuries of God's mercy, humans would hold back for fear of spending; Keep vigil (tahajjud) with recitation in part of the night as an extra devotion; The prophet may be raised to a 'praised station' (maqam mahmud), later read as intercession; Prayer: 'Lord, make my entrance and my exit true and grant me a helping authority'; Prayer is fixed from the sun's decline to the dark of night, with the dawn recitation; and 12 more.

matches.label: A holy vessel is described by its planks and their fastenings
matches.note: A holy vessel described by what it is made of: Šulgi R addresses Ninlil's barge part by part, 'your floor-planks (ĝiš-eme-sig) are flood-currents ... your side-planks, fastened (keše2) into their places with wooden rings' (A:15-16). Noah is carried 'on a thing of planks and fastenings (dhāti alwāḥin wa-dusur)' that 'runs under our eyes' (54:13-14). Both vessels were ordered by the deity (Ninlil commanded the barge, A:1-5); the Quran names the ark only by its planks and fastenings, while the hymn turns each part into an image.

evidence.text: Shared motifs, rarest first: The moon god renews his light, born every month, light of heaven and earth (weight 6.1); The god's utterance cannot be changed or overturned (weight 5.4). Pair score 11.5.

Only in Ibbi-Suen A: tigi to Suen, who makes Ibbi-Suen canal inspector of the Land: Praise is offered to the four great gods An, Enlil, Enki (Nudimmud) and the mother goddess Nintur; The god appoints the king as canal inspector (ku6-ĝal2) of the land; The high god names the king with a good name at his birth or accession.

Only in Syncretistic Hymn to Marduk 18-60: 'Your name is Anšar ... Dagan ... Adad ... Šamaš ... your name is indeed Marduk': Syncretistic litany: each great god (Anšar, Dagan, Adad, Nannar, Šamaš, Erra, Ningirsu) is declared to be a name or aspect of the one supreme god: 'your name is X ... your name is indeed Marduk'; The supreme god alone holds the rope (ṣerretu) or bond of heaven and earth, his sceptre laid across the netherworld; YHWH rides on a swift cloud and comes to Egypt; Egypt's idols tremble before him; How thunder in the clouds relates to the god: his own roar or a creature praising him [shared matter] [divergence between the texts]; Whatever name is pronounced, it belongs to the one god: 'he is our god' / 'his are the beautiful names' [divergence between the texts]; The god is creator of everything, without whom nothing whatsoever was formed and no lord could exist; The god's command cannot be altered and his assent cannot be changed; The god (alone) holds the heavens (and earth) in place: the bond or rope of heaven, holding back the sky; At the storm god's roar from the clouds heaven and earth shake, mountains quake and the seas are stirred up; Each line of a litany is repeated for one god under several names (Ninurta, Pabilsaĝ, Ninĝirsu), identifying them; The gods come and prostrate themselves before the victorious warrior god and greet him; The sun god is the king of justice who illuminates the land like a torch and assures the king's just rule; and 2 more.

Only in Ibbi-Suen B: šir-namgala to the twin gods Mešlamta-ea and Lugal-era, lords of the River Ordeal: Seven divine powers (me) adorn a god or temple; The princes of the underworld bow down to a god who sheds light in the abyss; The warrior god heaps up the enemies in piles; The god is a great neck-stock that weighs on the evil man; Hymnic refrain to the king: 'Who is as mighty as you, who rivals you?'; The divine River of the Ordeal (Id-lurugu) clears the just man and catches the evil; 'Who is like you among the gods, YHWH?'.

Only in Psalm 5 - morning prayer against the deceitful: The petitioner prays and sets out his case in the morning and waits; The enemies' throat is an open grave; they flatter with their tongue; The petitioner addresses God as 'my King and my God'; God is called the speaker's shield (magen); Speaker bows down toward God's holy temple (direction of prayer); Superscription contains an obscure musical or liturgical term (neginot, nehilot, sheminit, gittit, alamot, shiggayon, maskil, miktam, shoshannim...); Superscription 'for the leader/choirmaster' (lamenatseah); Psalm superscription ascribes the poem to David (le-david).

Only in Assur temple ritual - Aššur and the gods go to Bīt-Dagan; offerings in the palace courtyard; mouth-washing on day 23: Named gods, divine chariots and divine weapons travel with the chief god from his temple to another shrine; The mouth-washing rite (mīs pî) is performed for divine images; The goddess's offering portions are given to officials, palace women or the crown prince; Within a temple rite the king or priest makes a kispu, the food offering for the dead; The priest goes round the whole temple and its shrines during the rite; The god's house is gone round (circumambulated) as a rite; The king himself performs the temple rite: he sets the table, strews salt, slaughters the sheep and completes the libation; Temple doors, daises, braziers, city gates, the god's weapons and crown are written with the divine determinative and invoked or fed as gods; Colophon: 'written according to its original and collated'.

וַ֠יִּקְחוּ אֶת הַפָּ֨ר אֲשֶׁר נָתַ֣ן לָהֶם֮ וַֽיַּעֲשׂוּ֒ וַיִּקְרְא֣וּ בְשֵׁם הַ֠בַּעַל מֵהַבֹּ֨קֶר וְעַד הַצָּהֳרַ֤יִם לֵאמֹר֙ הַבַּ֣עַל עֲנֵ֔נוּ וְאֵ֥ין ק֖וֹל וְאֵ֣ין עֹנֶ֑ה וַֽיְפַסְּח֔וּ עַל הַמִּזְבֵּ֖חַ אֲשֶׁ֥ר עָשָֽׂה

(18:28) וַֽיִּקְרְאוּ֙ בְּק֣וֹל גָּד֔וֹל וַיִּתְגֹּֽדְדוּ֙ כְּמִשְׁפָּטָ֔ם בַּחֲרָב֖וֹת וּבָֽרְמָחִ֑ים עַד שְׁפָךְ דָּ֖ם עֲלֵיהֶֽם (18:29) וַֽיְהִי֙ כַּעֲבֹ֣ר הַֽצָּהֳרַ֔יִם וַיִּֽתְנַבְּא֔וּ עַ֖ד לַעֲל֣וֹת הַמִּנְחָ֑ה וְאֵֽין ק֥וֹל וְאֵין עֹנֶ֖ה וְאֵ֥ין קָֽשֶׁב

sides.note: 'according to their custom'; they prophesy until the offering time

evidence.text: Shared motifs, rarest first: Prophets of Baal limp-dance around the altar and gash themselves with swords and lances till blood flows (weight 7.7). Pair score 7.7.

Only in Iddin-Dagan A: the procession of cross-dressed and blood-spattering cult personnel before Inana: Cult personnel with swords and daggers spatter blood, and blood is poured on the dais before the goddess; From the midst of heaven the goddess looks down with joy on the people, numerous as sheep; Cult personnel of the goddess tighten their hairgrips and adorn their locks with coloured cloth; Young men wearing neck-stocks sing in the goddess's procession; Cult personnel parade before the goddess dressed in men's clothing on the right side and women's on the left; Woman must not wear man's gear, nor man a woman's garment; Participants in the goddess's procession carry swords, sword-belts and spears, 'the strength of battle'; Liturgical procession into the sanctuary with singers, musicians and maidens playing drums.

Only in Contest on Mount Carmel: Prophet repairs the ruined altar with twelve stones for the tribes of Jacob; Contest of gods: the god who answers by fire on an unlit sacrifice is God; The prophets of Baal are seized and slaughtered at the brook Kishon; Prophet mocks the silent god: perhaps he is musing, relieving himself, travelling, or asleep and must be woken; Sacrifice and altar drenched with four jars of water three times, filling a trench, before the miracle; The people fall on their faces crying 'YHWH, he is God! YHWH, he is God!'; How a public contest between God's prophet and the king's religious specialists ends [contrast between the texts]; An offering consumed by fire as proof of the true God or messenger [response between the texts]; Fire from heaven falls and consumes the offering, wood, stones, dust and water; 'How long will you hop between two branches? If YHWH is God, follow him; if Baal, follow him'; A single prophet of YHWH stands against 450 prophets of Baal and 400 of Asherah; How the people respond to the prophet's challenge over Baal [divergence between the texts]; and 10 more.

Only in The defrauders: Sijjin and 'Illiyyun: Woe to the defrauders (mutaffifin) who exact full measure from others but give short measure or weight; The record of the wicked is in Sijjin, that of the righteous in 'Illiyyun, each an inscribed book (kitab marqum) witnessed by those brought near; Sinners laughed at and winked at believers; on that day the believers laugh at the unbelievers from their couches; What they earned has covered their hearts with rust (rana); Deniers dismiss the recited signs as 'tales of the ancients' (asatir al-awwalin); On that day the wicked are veiled (debarred) from their Lord; An elite of 'those brought near' (al-muqarrabun) witness the righteous register and drink from Tasnim; Fraud by tampering with a measure [neutral] [divergence between the texts]; Not diminishing the measure and not tampering with the weights of the balance, tied to a day of reckoning; A written register in which servants are entered as faithful or unfaithful [divergence between the texts]; The record of the wicked is in Sijjin, that of the righteous in 'Illiyyun, each an inscribed book (kitab marqum) witnessed by those brought near [divergence between the texts]; The righteous drink sealed pure wine (rahiq makhtum) whose seal is musk; and 13 more.

Only in Rim-Sîn D: prayer to the gods of peace at the Great Gate of Urim as the king enters: The protective gods of peace who guard the city's Great Gate open the doors, rejoice at the king, carry his greeting to the gods and stand at his right and left; Named minor gods of a city gate are invoked one by one in a litany, each line beginning with the gate's name; Right (Niĝ-zid) and Justice (Niĝ-si-sa), personified as deities, are to be the king's helpers; Gods are asked to set favourable signs and encouraging words before the king and make his feet stand in holy places of life; A good protective spirit goes ahead and a protective goddess walks behind; A god is asked to speak a favourable word for the king to his wife in the temple.

Only in Rim-Sîn D: prayer to the gods of peace at the Great Gate of Urim as the king enters: The protective gods of peace who guard the city's Great Gate open the doors, rejoice at the king, carry his greeting to the gods and stand at his right and left; Named minor gods of a city gate are invoked one by one in a litany, each line beginning with the gate's name; Right (Niĝ-zid) and Justice (Niĝ-si-sa), personified as deities, are to be the king's helpers; Gods are asked to set favourable signs and encouraging words before the king and make his feet stand in holy places of life; A good protective spirit goes ahead and a protective goddess walks behind; A god is asked to speak a favourable word for the king to his wife in the temple.

Only in Nearer than the jugular vein; the two recorders; driver and witness; Gehenna says 'Is there more?'; creation in six days without weariness: On the day the caller calls from a place near at hand, and they hear the Cry (al-sayha): the day of coming forth; The damned man's companion (qarin) disputes before God: 'Our Lord, I did not make him transgress'; The earth splits open from them and they hasten forth to the gathering; 'Enter it in peace': the day of eternity; they have what they wish and more (mazid) with God; The Garden is brought near to the God-fearing, not far off; God created the heavens and earth in six days and no weariness (lughub) touched him; Every soul comes with a driver (sa'iq) and a witness (shahid); The stupor (sakra) of death comes with the truth: 'this is what you tried to avoid'; Two receivers sit on the right and the left recording every word a person utters; At judgment the covering is removed from a person and his sight that day is sharp as iron; Whether the work of creation brings toil and weariness on the divine [divergence between the texts]; Whether the work of creation brings toil and weariness on the divine [response between the texts]; and 25 more.

matches.note: Sumerian dal-ba-na ḫur-saĝ 2-a-bi 'between the two mountain ranges' against Arabic bayna s-saddayn 'between the two barriers'. sides.note: A building whose top reaches the midst of heaven. Enlil's E-kur is praised for it, its radiance touching heaven; Pharaoh's ṣarḥ, meant to reach heaven and look at the God of Moses, is his evil deed made fair to him.

passages.text: וַיֹּאמְר֞וּ הָ֣בָה נִבְנֶה לָּ֣נוּ עִ֗יר וּמִגְדָּל֙ וְרֹאשׁ֣וֹ בַשָּׁמַ֔יִם וְנַֽעֲשֶׂה לָּ֖נוּ שֵׁ֑ם פֶּן נָפ֖וּץ עַל פְּנֵ֥י כָל הָאָֽרֶץ
וַיֵּ֣רֶד יְהוָ֔ה לִרְאֹ֥ת אֶת הָעִ֖יר וְאֶת הַמִּגְדָּ֑ל אֲשֶׁ֥ר בָּנ֖וּ בְּנֵ֥י הָאָדָֽם
וַיָּ֨פֶץ יְהוָ֥ה אֹתָ֛ם מִשָּׁ֖ם עַל פְּנֵ֣י כָל הָאָ֑רֶץ וַֽיַּחְדְּל֖וּ לִבְנֹ֥ת הָעִֽיר

sides.note: A tower toward heaven: Babel's builders, all humankind (hāvâ nivneh llānû ʿîr û-migdāl wə-rōʾšô vaš-šāmayim), want to make a name and not be scattered; God comes down to see, and scatters them. In the Quran one king orders it of his minister (fa-jʿal lī ṣarḥan laʿallī aṭṭaliʿu ilā ilāhi Mūsā wa-innī la-aẓunnuhu mina l-kādhibīna): the aim is to climb up and look at Moses' God, mockingly. The ending is drowning (fa-nabadhnāhum fī l-yamm), not dispersal. God's descent to inspect the tower (wa-yyēred YHWH lirʾōt) is reversed into Pharaoh's wish to ascend and inspect God.

passages.text: وَقَالَ فِرْعَوْنُ يَٰٓأَيُّهَا ٱلْمَلَأُ مَا عَلِمْتُ لَكُم مِّنْ إِلَٰهٍ غَيْرِى فَأَوْقِدْ لِى يَٰهَٰمَٰنُ عَلَى ٱلطِّينِ فَٱجْعَل لِّى صَرْحًا لَّعَلِّىٓ أَطَّلِعُ إِلَىٰٓ إِلَٰهِ مُوسَىٰ وَإِنِّى لَأَظُنُّهُۥ مِنَ ٱلْكَٰذِبِينَ
وَٱسْتَكْبَرَ هُوَ وَجُنُودُهُۥ فِى ٱلْأَرْضِ بِغَيْرِ ٱلْحَقِّ وَظَنُّوٓا۟ أَنَّهُمْ إِلَيْنَا لَا يُرْجَعُونَ
فَأَخَذْنَٰهُ وَجُنُودَهُۥ فَنَبَذْنَٰهُمْ فِى ٱلْيَمِّ فَٱنظُرْ كَيْفَ كَانَ عَٰقِبَةُ ٱلظَّٰلِمِينَ

sides.note: A tower toward heaven: Babel's builders, all humankind (hāvâ nivneh llānû ʿîr û-migdāl wə-rōʾšô vaš-šāmayim), want to make a name and not be scattered; God comes down to see, and scatters them. In the Quran one king orders it of his minister (fa-jʿal lī ṣarḥan laʿallī aṭṭaliʿu ilā ilāhi Mūsā wa-innī la-aẓunnuhu mina l-kādhibīna): the aim is to climb up and look at Moses' God, mockingly. The ending is drowning (fa-nabadhnāhum fī l-yamm), not dispersal. God's descent to inspect the tower (wa-yyēred YHWH lirʾōt) is reversed into Pharaoh's wish to ascend and inspect God.

evidence.text: Shared motifs, rarest first: At the New Year festival of Dumuzid the underworld pipes are opened, memorial libations poured, and priests and the dead eat and drink to keep away ghosts (weight 7.7). Pair score 7.7.

Only in A hymn to Inana as Ninegala (Inana D), part 1, the astral goddess, her seats and her ways: The goddess slips through thornbushes, strides the mountains, drinks from puddles with dogs and shares the stall with horses; The mother of a sick child lays her child in the goddess's arms; A deity goes out (up into the mountains) to detect falsehood and justice and tell the criminal from the just; The astral goddess appears like moonlight at night and like sunlight at noon; The high god's consort decides destinies together with him and is the pleasure of his heart; he embraces her; Inana (evening star) is the prostitute who goes to the tavern and is food to the poor; The goddess rides on a lion or great beast; A son pours clean water for his dead father and mother: 'drink clean water!'; Inana is titled lady, queen or mother of heaven (nin/ama an-na, 'queen of heaven'); Each stanza is sung twice, the second time naming the deity or king (litany-like repetition); The king, as the goddess's bridegroom (Dumuzid), lies with Inana, who then decrees his fate.

Only in Return through the seven gates; the ransom; Tammuz bathed and dressed; Belili's cry; the dead come up to smell the incense (Ishtar's Descent 119-138): Tammuz (Dumuzi) is bathed, anointed and dressed in red; wailing men and women and the lapis flute accompany his annual coming up, and the dead come up to smell the incense; The released goddess must pay a ransom (napṭiru) or be brought back to the netherworld; The dying god's sister (Belili / Geshtinanna) hears the wailing for her brother and cries 'Do not rob me of my only brother!'; No one leaves the underworld unscathed: one who ascends must provide a substitute in her place; The underworld has seven gates, bolted and opened one at a time.

Shared motifs, rarest first: Heaven and earth placed on, or held in, the deity's head, hand or feet (weight 7.3). Pair score 7.3.

Only in A hymn to Inana (Inana F), Inana's self-praise (Emesal): When the goddess enters the high god's temple the gatekeeper does not stop her and the minister does not tell her to rise; Litany in which the deity claims a list of named temples in named cities, each 'is mine'; The sky god, afraid of the goddess, seats her in his dwelling and hands over to her the royal and divine rites; A goddess (or her attendants) speaks in Emesal, the register of Sumerian used for goddesses and women; Boast: the other gods are small birds, I am the falcon; the gods butt one another, I am the wild cow; The high god sets heaven on the goddess's head as a crown and puts the earth on her feet as sandals; Hymnic refrain to the king: 'Who is as mighty as you, who rivals you?'.

Only in Do not despair of mercy; the earth in God's grip; the throngs to hell and Garden: The angels are seen surrounding the Throne, glorifying the praise of their Lord; The blessed praise God who gave them the land (ard) as inheritance to settle in the Garden where they will; The Book (record) is laid down, the prophets and witnesses are brought, and judgment is passed with truth; Unbelievers are driven to hell in throngs (zumar) and the godfearing to the Garden in throngs; the gates open and the keepers address each; The keepers of the Garden greet the righteous 'Peace be upon you, you have been good; enter'; Lest a soul say 'Alas for my neglect of God' or 'If only I had another chance (karra)'; If you associate partners with God your deeds will come to nothing; At the first trumpet blast all in heaven and earth swoon (sa'iqa) except whom God wills; at the second they stand looking; On the Day of Resurrection the whole earth is in God's grip and the heavens folded in his right hand; The earth shines (lit up) with God's glory; The earth shines (lit up) with God's glory [divergence between the texts]; At the gate of the netherworld the gatekeepers question those who arrive [divergence between the texts]; and 14 more.

evidence.text: Read side by side in both originals (alignments/ane-quran/06-ane-quran.yaml).
Shared motifs, rarest first: 'If only (the enemy / the wrongdoers) knew or saw' the god's strength (formula) (weight 7.7). Pair score 7.7.

matches.label: How the parents' word stands to the word of God
matches.note: Both join the parents to the deity in one precept: Šuruppag sets the mother's word beside the personal god's word, and says the mother is like Utu who gives birth and the father like a god whose word is true. 31:14-15 joins thanks to God and to the parents (with the mother's bearing, ḥamalathu ummuhu), then limits obedience: if they strive to make you associate, do not obey them. Only in One fate for all; the living dog; eat your bread with joy: The living know they will die, but the dead know nothing, have no more reward, and their love, hate and envy have perished; Whatever your hand finds to do, do with your might, for there is no work, reckoning, knowledge or wisdom in Sheol; The righteous and the wise and their deeds are in the hand of God; whether love or hate, man does not know; One fate for righteous and wicked, clean and unclean, him who sacrifices and him who does not, the one who swears and the one who fears an oath; One fate (miqreh) befalls the wise and the fool, man and beast alike; Go, eat your bread with joy and drink your wine; let your garments always be white and oil not lack on your head; enjoy life with the woman you love; There is nothing better than to eat, drink and find enjoyment in one's toil; this is from the hand of God.

matches.label: Dream of sun, moon and eleven stars bowing to the hero
matches.note: A son reports to his parent a night dream of the stars of heaven (kakkabū šamāʾī; kawkab), with homage in it, and the parent interprets: Ninsun 'who knows everything' (mūdât kalāma) and Jacob, who sees in it God's choosing (yajtabīka rabbuka) and the teaching of interpretation. Changed: the homage. In Gilgameš the young men of the land kiss the feet of the fallen star-rock (eṭlūtum unaššaqū šēpīšu), which stands for the coming friend; in 12:4 the stars, sun and moon prostrate to the dreamer himself (lī sājidīn), fulfilled when his family falls down before him (12:100). The meaning: a companion to be loved like a wife, against a destiny to be kept from jealous brothers.

matches.label: Knowledge of the flood age, hidden from people, is brought to them
matches.note: The flood story is framed as hidden knowledge brought to people who did not have it: the hero 'saw the secret and uncovered the hidden, brought back a report (ṭēmu) from before the Deluge'; 11:49, closing Noah's story, 'these are tidings of the unseen (anbāʾ al-ghayb) that we reveal to you; you did not know them, nor your people, before this'. Changed: who brings it and how. Gilgameš fetches it by travelling to Ūta-napišti and sets it on a stele; the Prophet receives it by revelation.

Only in Šamḫat describes Uruk and tells Gilgameš's dreams of the star and the axe (Gilgameš SB I): The city is praised as a place of daily festival, drums and comely harlots; Dreams foretell the arrival of a mighty companion who will be the hero's friend and saviour; A dream of a star or rock fallen from the sky that the dreamer cannot lift, and which he loves like a wife; The hero loves his male friend 'like a wife', caressing and embracing him; The hero's wise divine mother interprets his dreams for him; A dream given twice means God has firmly decided and will act soon; The newly civilised wild man resolves to go to the city and challenge its overbearing king; The sun god is the king's brother and friend, guardian of his weapons, who shines on him in battle; Each figure and object of a symbolic dream is identified in turn by the interpreter (the man is X, the woman is Y).

Only in Joseph and his brothers (Surah 12, full read): Brothers tell their father to ask the town and the caravan to confirm their story; Brothers claim the accused youth's absent brother (the hero) had also stolen before; Famished brothers bring poor goods and ask the disguised hero for alms; The brothers confess 'we were sinners' once the hero is revealed and ask their father to pray for them; Father keeps lamenting his lost son for years until his sons fear he will waste away; The patriarch claims to know from God what his sons do not know; Father promises his repentant sons to ask God's forgiveness for them later; Fleeing the seductress, the hero and the woman find her husband at the door; The bereaved father answers with 'beautiful patience' (sabr jamil) and reliance on God; The hero could not have kept his brother under the king's law, so a stratagem is needed; The hero declares he follows the religion of his fathers Abraham, Isaac and Jacob; A camel-load is promised to whoever brings back the missing royal cup, with a guarantor; and 146 more.
